speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I desire to call your attention to a matter which was brought to the attention of the House on -Friday last by the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). The Prime Minister referred to an article which has appeared in a Toronto paper in which no names were mentioned. Since that time articles have appeared in other papers in which my name is mentioned. I have not yet had an opportunity to consider these articles, but I hope to be able to make some observations in the matter to-morrow.

I notice a paragraph in ' La Patrie ' of Saturday about the commanding officers of the Coronation Contingent in which it is stated that Hon. Mr. Brodeur and Hon. Mr. Lemieux objected so strenuously in council to the appointment of Lt.-Col. Landry that Sir Frederick Borden was forced to appoint another commanding officer belonging to the Liberal party. I may say that this paragraph, from beginning to end, is without foundation in fact. Lt.-Col. Landry is a personal friend of mine, indeed a college mate of mine. His name never came before me in connection with this matter, and I had nothing to do with the selection of the commanding officer of the Coronation Contingent; in fact, this is the first time I have heard his name mentioned in this connection.
May I ask the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) whether or not the return I spoke of the other day has been prepared?
It has. I have signed it, and I thought it would have been here. I will see that it is brought down before the House rise's.
I desire to ask the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) if he has yet given the additions which were asked for in relation to the curator's report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There were some supplementary papers, which I thought had been submitted to the House. But, I find they have not been. I will have them printed to-morrow.

I would like to ask the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) if the remainder of the return that was asked for-part was nut as a question and part stood as a notice of motion for- return-in relation to trade statistics of the most favoured nations and the tariffs on goods going into those countries, is yet ready?
I have not this yet, but I will have inquiry made this afternoon about it.

["This subject of immigration is one of great interest, but in the discussion of the last hour and a ha'.f it has been one of great disappointment also. I have never given great attention 'to (the study of immigration statistics, but, reading newspaper reports, and listening to the statements of the Minister of the Interior, I have been lead for years to believe that we were gaining, through our immigration system, very large additions to our population, and very considerably so from the United States-at a cost to us of a good deal of money. The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) has thrown some light on that matter this afternoon. He has taken the settlers' effects as a", 'guide. He read from the Trade and Navigation returns showing that last year\'s settlers\' effects from the United States to Canada amounted to $7,613,500, and that settlers\' effects from Canada to the United States amounted to $2,076,000. I can well understand the large amount of settlers\' effects from the United States into Canada, because the arrivals from the United States in our western provinces almost always carry large quantities of farm machinery, horses, cattle, wagons, &c. But, to my mind, the Minister of Customs may be a litt\'le out of the way when he makes the value of settlers\' effects the basis of a comparison showing the number of people coming into and going out of the country. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) spoke of the migration from the maritime provinces to the United States. From the character of that migration, I should suppose the people going from the maritime provinces had taken very litt\'le with them, whereas the people going into the western provinces from the United States bring a great deal. I think it would not be too much to say that the value of the settlers\' effects coming into Canada would be three times as much for the average individual as the value of settler\'s effects carried by the people from the maritime provinces going into the United States. That may be even a little under the mark. If, for the sake of the comparison, we say that the people coming from the United States into our west bring $3.50 in settlers\' effects for every $1 that is taken out by our people going from the maritime provinces to the United States, we find that practically we have an equal movement of emigration and immigration. I am a little afraid that that is really the case,-that we are losing just as much as we are gaining. We shall have to await the census returns to see if that can be verified or not. But it does look as though, while the minister is spending a great deal of money and filling up the western country at what we might ca\'ll the bung-hole, he is neglecting to see how much is running out of the spout from the maritime provinces. From what has been said this afternoon, I am very much afraid that our net gain is very little. I hope the Minister of the Interior will, even if it costs more, carry out some system of keep-" ing track of the people that go out of the country. It cannot be expected that this is to be done without money; but I am not aware that this parliament ever refuses any reasonable appropriation for any purpose of correct and useful statistics. The subject is so interesting and important, that I am sure parliament would gladly provide the money. I was much surprised to learn that no real account is kept of the people going out of the country as well 257\nas those coming in. The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) referred to what had occurred about twenty years ago and what was said on the matter. We a\'ll remember the howl of Sir Richard Cartwright, particularly with regard to the exodus. He magnified it to such an extent that I believe he got away beyond the bounds. He talked about the people we were losing and about there being a million native born Canadians in the United States at that time. I do not know whether he got his figures from the American returns or not, but I always thought he magnified them, and magnified them for a purpose. He did it to show that the National Policy had failed. And we have the National Policy to-day, with what hon. gentlemen opposite say are improvements made in it by themselves, yet the population seems to be going out of the country as fast as it was then. I merely rise to voice my opinion in favour of the Minister of the Interior taking steps to get for the future more correct statistics than he has been getting with regard to the people leaving the country.\nIt would be just as interesting to us to know whether we are losing population as to know whether we are gaining it. My opinion is that we are lbsing about as much as we are getting, so far as the United States are concerned. No doubt the figures furnished us by the Department of the Interior axe fairly correct of the number of people coming in from Great Britain and European countries. We are not losing people going across the water. I trust the minister will take the necessary steps to inform us in the future as to the movement of population both ways, not only from the United States into Canada, but from Canada into the United States.']

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I would like to read a couple of press despatches and call the attention of the government to a matter of some interest to all Canadians. The first despatch is as follows:

Canada's Piece Cut Out as Objectionable to Americans.
London, April 25.-It was learned to-day that it was in consequence of communications between London and Washington, and hints to the Canadian committee, of which Lord Strathcona is president, that a decision is reached to eliminate from the coronation programme Canada's principal contribution to the pageantry 'Festival of the Empire.' The piece which has been in course of preparation at the Crystal Palace, and which called for 600 performers, entitled 'Chateau-guay, where Canada was held for the empire,' was intended to represent the defeat of the invading American force in 1812 by a handful of Canadians.
After consideration it was thought that the pageant might wound the susceptibilities of American visitors to the coronation, and it was also suggested that a feeling might be caused in the United States that would endanger the conclusion of the proposed Anglo-
American arbitration treaty. Rather than make either event possible the authorities decided to abandon the spectacle.
In a later despatch among several which I have here there is an extract from the London ' Standard ' which reads as follows:
The Canadians have an incontestable ri*ht to occupy a very prominent and honourable place in the commemoration of the great deeds of empire. This particular incident, a happy selection in many ways, was not a British but a Canadian victory, which was to be fitly celebrated without the least wish to wound American sentiment. We cannot but regret that the scene has been omitted from the pageant at the last moment.
I do not know whether there has been an official programme of the Pageant of Empire issued, but I lam sure that it is of interest to all Canadians to know what form Canada's participation in that great spectacle will take and I am also certain that it would be a matter of great gratification to all Canadians to know that the battle of Chateauguay was to be represented in the festival. The House is familiar with the details of that celebrated episode, one, not only of the most brilliant and most heroic, but one of the most decisive battles, with Lundy's Lane, in the whole war of 1812, a war, Sir, which we all know was one distinctly of defence when Canadians of all nationalities met for the common defence of their homes, their soil, * and their institutions. I am not going to refer to the details of that encounter but we know perfectly well that it was less than a thousand French Canadians who, under de Salaberry, the gallant leader of the French Canadians, and the equally gallant Macdonald of Glengarry, who, by superior strategy and valour, defeated an overwhelming force of Americans at that time. As I have said, it was a war, not of aggression but of defence. This is literally true as far as Canadians are concerned, and I feel that every member of the House, and every Canadian, recognizes now that it had the most beneficent influence upon Canada's future, because, for the first time, that war, whatever its unjustifiable features may have been, welded together French, English, Scotch, and Irish. All were animated by one common spirit and by the noblest patriotism. I am quite sure that we all agree that stirring incidents of this kind which mark the special epochs in our national development should be commemorated and recognized by all Canadians. It has been finely said that as Canadians look down the corridors of time they will always see the flashes of the musketry and cannon of Lundy's Lane and hear the bugles blow which drove the invaders from
*8107

*the woods of Chateauguay. For these reasons, it is a matter of great regret that a decision has been come to to eliminate a spectacle of this kind at the Festival of Empire, where all races and all portions of the empire will be represented to celebrate the empire's heroic deeds. Neither can I think the House will come to the conclusion that the reasons given for the elimination of the pageant of the battle of Chateauguay are sufficient. We know that in New England there was a general condemnation of that war and I feel sure that the American people have long ago buried any feeling of animosity they entertained at one time. I might point out indeed that our good friends on the south of the line, for whom we have the kindliest feelings, occasionally, not only celebrate victories on their own soil, but come over to ours. In my own town many of our American friends have come over and celebrated the fourth of July right under our noses and on our own territory, and none of us felt any the worse for it. I am inclined to take with a grain of salt, the idea of wounding the feelings of the American people by celebrating the battle of Chateauguay. No Canadian would Te-sent the fact that the Americans celebrate the battle of Hunker's Hill, if they desire to commemorate their own national achievements, and I am sure our American friends would take our celebration of the battle of Chateauguay in the same spirit. If we are to admit the principle that we cannot celebrate national achievements because it hurts the feelingsi of somebody then we might just as well cut out all celebrations of the kind. I take it that the government has been consulted with reference to these great pageants, and I would like the Prime Minister or the Minister of Agriculture, who sometimes has charge of these things, to explain how it is that an historic event of this kind, dear to the heart of every Canadian and recognized as an noble achievement in Canadian history, is to be eliminated at a time like this when every great deed in the empire's history is to be held up to the admiration of our people.

The Battle of Chateauguay is one of the historic events in which Canadians have always taken pride, but I may inform my hon. friend that the pageants at the Festival of Empire are under the control and management of the committee in London, and the Canadian government has not been consulted with reference to them. What information we have on the matter is such as my hon. friend has seen in the public press, and whether that is correct or not I cannot say. We are taking part in the Festival of Empire but not Mr. BURRELL
in any of the particular pageants which have been proposed by the authorities of the Festival in London. I believe that Lord Strathcona is a member of the executive or management of the Festival of Empire, but just what part he has taken in regard to the pageant I do not know. Whatever he has done in that respect he * has done as Lord Strathcona, and not as the High Commissioner for Canada.

Am I to understand that
the government of Canada has not contributed, financially or morally or in any other way?

We are contributing for the general expenses of the Festival of Empire, and possibly part of that may be devoted to the pageants, but the money is put into the hands of the committee in London for their purpose, and I do not know how it has been distributed. We are erecting a Canadian building which will have an exhibit of Canadian products and Canadian resources.
If the government is very anxious as to how the public money is expended it does seem to me that in an event of this kind they might insist on being consulted.

I am very glad that my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) has brought this up. When I read the news item, it struck me as rather-I scarcely knew what word to express it-but I felt that Canada had hardly been used right. History is history, and those who are in charge of pageantry by which history is supposed to be truthfully delineated ought not on such an occasion as this to omit one of the most important and illustrious events in our Canadian history. It does not seem to me that the people of the United States would be likely to be in any way offended by this pageant being carried out true to history. I should not like to think so ill of our friends on the south of the line as to think they would take the least umbrage at seeing a truthful delineation of Canadian history. It seems to me that the omission is pandering to a rather mawkish kind of sentimentality.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) read the American school books upon the Battle of Chateauguay?
* Mr. FOSTER. Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not represented in them as a Canadian victory.

Then still less should they take objection to it. If my right hon. friend has read the old school books and old histories he probably may have read the new, and he will find that in the last ten or fifteen years the version of these

old occurrences between ourselves and the United States has been very greatly modified in being more true to the fact.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not read the new books, but I know that in the old American school books the Battle of Chateauguay was never represented as a Canadian victory. For my part, I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) that this should not be a reason to eliminate the true character of that battle, for I believe that the Americans understand that history is history as has been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Foster). But the matter has been decided; it has not been referred to us, and really officially we have nothing to do with it. We contributed our money to the Festival of Empire which was placed in the hands of the London Committee and perhaps the committee has decided in this way. Had I been a member of the committee I would have decided otherwise.

I desire to call the attention of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs to a fact of very great importance to the administration of justice in the province of Manitoba. It will be remembered that some little time ago, while I was discussing the St. Peter's Indian reserve and asking for a Royal Commission to investigate that matter, the Minister of the Interior referred me to the government of Manitoba and said that if there was any prosecution or any investigation it should be made by the government of Manitoba. Other speakers on that side of the House made the same statement. The province of Manitoba guarantees all titles issued under the Torrens system and before the Registrar General of Manitoba can guarantee those titles he must be satisfied that the titles are good. The Indians allege that this surrender was obtained illegally and that the lands, after they had been given to them, were taken from them illegally. Consequently the Registrar General refuses to issue titles until there is a thorough investigation which will place him in a position to say whether or not the title is vested in the present holders. To that end, the government of Manitoba have appointed a Royal Commission for the purpose of determining whether or not the titles are good, and whether the Registrar General would be justified in guaranteeing them. To enable the commission to arrive at a proper conclusion it is necessary that they should have the original documents regarding this surrender. Serious allegations have been made by the Indians. On the strength of these allegations I myself stated in this House that forgery had been committed in the signing of receipts for the patents. This matter cannot be established
unless the commission has the original documents. The counsel for the Royal Commission has written to me the following letter which I wish to place on ' Hansard ':
Winnipeg, Canada,
19th April, 1911.
Dear Sir,-I have the honour to inclose you copy of letter written by me as counsel for the Royal Commission appointed to investigate the surrender of the St. Peter's reserve addressed to the Hon. Frank Oliver, Minister of the Interior. I also inclose you his reply thereto. Both letters are self-explanatory.
It is absolutely essential that the commission should have production of the original documents in regard to the surrender of this reserve, and since the Minister of the Interior suggests that an order of parliament should he obtained I take the liberty of requesting that you should move for an order of parliament for production of the original documents in connection with this matter before the Royal Commission. Will you be kind enough to advise me of the result.
Yours truly,
H. W. WHITLA, Counsel for the Commission. Geo. H. Bradbury, Esq., M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
I have here a copy of a letter written by the counsel for the commission to the hon. the Minister of the Interior:
Winnipeg, Canada,
12th April, 1911.
Dear Sir,-By order of the Executive Council of the province of Manitoba a commission has been appointed to investigate and report upon the surrender of the St. Peter's Indian reserve.
The commission has instructed me as counsel to request the production of the records of the Indian Office in relation to that particular reserve. Upon application to Mr. Sem-mens this morning he stated he would require some authority before he could permit either an inspection or production of the documents. I therefore take the liberty of writing you to ask if you will be good enough to instruct Mr. Semmens, or the agent in charge of the Winnipeg office, to permit an inspection by and to produce to the proper agent of the commissioners all the documents relating to the surrender of the Indian reserve. Trusting that you will see your way clear to give this necessary authority,
I am, vours respectfully,
(Sgd.) H. W. WHITLA, Counsel for the Commission. Hon. Frank Oliver,
Minister of the Interior, c/o Royal Alexandra Hotel,
City.
H.W.W./R.
The Minister of the Interior replies as follows:
Winnipeg, April 12, 1911
Dear Sir,-Yours of the 12th of April to hand requesting inspection by a commission appointed by the government of Manitoba of

papers connected with the surrender of the St. Peter's Indian reserve.	.
In reply I beg to say that until otherwise advised, I am not aware that the government of Manitoba has authority to request an inspection of the documents in question.
All documents connected with the transaction of business by the government of Canada can properly be produced for inspection on an order of parliament or of the courts.
I would suggest that the commission take this means of securing the inspection desired.
Yours faithfully,

H. D. Whitla, Esq.,
Box 1556, Winnipeg, Man.
Mr. Speaker, my object in bringing this matter before the House is to have these documents produced. I realize that if I place this motion on the order paper, it may be days or weeks perhaps before it is reached, and as my only object is to facilitate the work of this commission-and I am sure that the minister must be as much interested as I or any other man in Canada to see that this matter is cleared up-I would ask the minister if he would accept an order of the House for the production of these papers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The facts in connection with this matter are as my hon. friend has stated. I am not desirous of in any way impeding the work of the commission appointed by the government of Manitoba, but, having a certain responsibility in regard to the custody of the documents, I would ask my hon. friend to let the matter rest until to-morrow, when I will be able to give him a definite answer.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I *wish again to direct the attention of the government to the subject of emigration from Canada to the United States to which I alluded last year. At page 5524 of ' Hansard,' of last year, I set forth a statement which appeared in the annual report of the Commissioner General of Immigration for the United States. It appeared from that report that the total immigration into the United States from Canada during the fiscal year ending June 30, 1909, was 96,520, and that, after eliminating certain portions of that immigration which could not be properly classed as actual immigration from Canada to the United States there was found to be a total immigration into the United States from Canada of 61,038, according to the returns made to the Commissioner General of Immigration of the United States and as embodied by him in that report. I also called attention to certain rather important statements in his report of that year, in which he gave reasons why the immigration into the United States from Mr. BRADBURY.
Canada had increased in bo marked a degree during the twelve months covered by his report.
I have now the report of the Commissioner General of Immigration for the United States which gives the returns up to June 30, 1910. According to these returns the emigration from the United States to Canada during the twelve months mentioned amounted to 116,377. The report classifies that emigration as follows:	United
States citizens, 78,697; Canadian citizens, 15,203; other aliens, 22,477; making a total of 116,377. During the same period the emigration from Canada to the United States, according to this report, was as follows: United States citizens, 22,832; Canadian citizens, 44,328; other aliens, 27,336; making a total of 94,496. If these statistics are correct, the balance of immigration into Canada from the United States over the emigration from Canada to the United States was a little less than 22,000, which result, I am bound to say, is one that I would hardly have expected. I do not know whether the hon. the Minister of the Interior has any observations to make on these statistics; I do not know whether they are accepted by the government as accurate. There does not appear to be any official information available in this country as to the number of persons leaving Canada for permanent residence in the United States. In other words, although we have very full, and I believe very complete statistics of immigration into this country, I do not know that we have any statistics of emigration from this country to the United States or elsewhere. Am I correct in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax;. Well, there may be difficulties in the way of obtaining and preserving such statistics, of which I am not aware, but otherwise I would be very much inclined to think that we might very well follow the example of the United States and compile and publish statistics not only of the immigration into this country, but of the emigration from this country. That is done in the United States *n a very complete way. Not only do they keep statistics of all the persons leaving that country, but they classify them as United States citizens, Canadian citizens, and other aliens, so far as those statistics relate to emigration from the United States to Canada. Similarly they divide the emigration from Canada, to the United States into three classes-United States citizens, Canadian citizens, and other aliens. I am bound to say that I think it would be greatly to the advantage of the country if we knew at the present time, as we do not seem to know, from what provinces of Canada, and in what proportion from those

provinces, this very large emigration of nearly 95,000 persons has gone during the fiscal year ended the 30th of June, 1910, if the figures of the United States Immigration Department are to be accepted as accurate. We know that at one time there was a very considerable emigration from Canada to the United States, especially from certain of the eastern provinces. We had been led to believe that that emigration had almost wholly ceased; but if these figures are even approximately correct, it is evident that our belief in that regard was not based on a very sure foundation, because it is rather astonishing to find that in a single year no less than 94,496 persons have left Canada for permanent residence in the United States, and that these figures comprise 44,328 Canadian citizens in addition to 22,832 United States citizens, and 27,336 aliens not being citizens of Canada.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: How do their figures of emigration from the United States to Canada compare with our figures?

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: It is a little difficult to compare them on account of the difference in the fiscal year. _ They give their figures for the year ending the 30th of June, while our figures are given for the year ending the 31st of March. In the United States returns they are given by months. I do not know whether or not ours are so given. However, I thought the matter worthy of some attention from the government, and, therefore, I have brought it to the notice of the House. I would be very glad if the Minister of the Interior would give us any observations which would indicate whether or not these figures are to be accepted as substantially accurate, and, further, whether there are in his opinion any serious difficulties in the way of inaugurating a system by which statistics of emigration as well as immigration may be compiled in this country in the future, for the information of parliament and the people.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: There is no doubt a considerable reciprocity in population between Canada and the United States, and has been for many years, and will continue to be. We try to keep account of the .people coming from the United States to Canada with the intention of residing in Canada. We think our figures are accurate or fairly accurate; but it must be quite evident that figures calculated as ours must be, cannot by any possibility be absolutely accurate; they can only be approximately so.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
How do our figures of immigration coming from the United States agree month by month with the United States figures of emigration from the United States?
Mr. OLIVER, I could not give my hon. friend a statement that would have serious value; but I am under the impression that there is a wide divergence between the figures, and it is easy to see how that divergence might take place. We may have one standard of calculation, and they may have an entirely different one. We may consider a person an immigrant, whom they would not rank as such. Their system may be more comprehensive than ours.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Is the basis the same?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I am satisfied that the basis is not the same.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: In what is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I am not able to give my hon. friend detailed information; lam speaking subject to correction in a general way. When the estimates were up for consideration, this matter was brought to my attention, and I pointed out to the committee then that it was quite possible to secure such information for Canada as was already secured for the United States. It would mean a very considerable increase in the cost of our immigration service and would not produce any immediate or direct beneficial result. So, up to the present time, we have not asked parliament for an appropriation to enable us to make such a count and calculation. It is a serious question for parliament to consider whether the value of the information would be equal to the cost. For my part I think that, up to the present time, we have been well advised to spend our money and energy in dealing with the people who are coming, rather than with the people who are going. We were not able to prevent them from going or we would do so. But by spending our money as we have been doing, we have been enabled, certainly, to bring people here and this has resulted in our material benefit. If a count of people going could reasonably be expected to result in the formulation of a policy that would prevent their going, I could see a sound reason for the expenditure. But unless and until some such policy is in near or further prospect, I should think it was a matter to seriously consider whether we could afford to put the money into the service or not. It will be understood by the House that people move sometimes because of the conditions in which they live, but most generally because of the conditions in the place to which they are going. That is to say, we attract people from the United States and Great Britain, and from other countries of Europe, not so much because of the conditions surrounding those people at home, as because of the advantages they hope to gain in coming to our country. So, the people who leave Canada for the United States,

we may reasonably presume, do not leave so much because of the conditions in Canada as because of the expectations they have of conditions in the United States. That being a matter that is not in our control, we cannot be sure that we should be able to frame a policy that would have any serious result, even if we had the information. That is the view that the department has he'ld up to the present time. We are prepared, of course, at any time, to take stock and count of the people who are going out, if parliament is so minded, and is prepared to supply the necessary funds.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I think that the minister (Mr. Oliver), if he will consider the matter a little, will see that there are a number of good reasons why we should have this information which we evidently lack, according to the figures and statements which have been made and presented by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). It is quite as important in its own way to know the stream of people that is leaving us, and from what quarters of the country it is leaving us, so as to get at the reasons for the stream going out from the country, as to know what population is coming to us, and the sources from which it comes. It' seems to me there are strong economic Teasons .for our knowing that state ,of facts, in order that we may find out. the causes of the outflowing stream. I do not think it would involve a great deal of added cost. You have your customs house officers and immigration officers, and they take charge of the stream that comes in, they trace it, number the individuals and forward their reports to the department. The places of ingress into the country, other things being equal, are the places of egress from the other country. Immigrants coming into Canada generally come with effects, and they have to pass the customs, so it is not difficult to keep count of them. Emigrants from this country also take personal effects, and they have to pass the customs line on the other side, and so it is not difficult to number them. But there is another consideration. We are buoyed up by the favourable information of one side only. Every year the minister tells us: Everything is going well; we are spending a great deal of money, but we are getting in many immigrants, settlers who are just that much added to the country.. But it would be a dffierent tale if the minister were to come down and tell us of the number that have left Canada. I do not recollect the numbers shown by our figures who have come in from the United States last year. But suppose we call it a hundred thousand,-I do not think it was one hundred thousand.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
We have been going on with the idea that we have attracted to us from the United States one hundred thousand people, and so are that much better off. But up comes the United States official-and their officials are well trained and their statistics far ahead of Canadian statistics-who says:	Yes, you did get somewhere near
one hundred thousand people from the United States, but ninety-four thousand came into the United States from Canada, so that the net gain is very small. We have been pluming ourselves upon despoiling our neighbours of a number of their eligible cultivators and other inhabitants, but it seems to be without any real reason. Now, does not the minister think that in the interest of true knowledge and for the purpose of obtaining complete statistics, which will set forth all the important facts on both sides-and these statistics alone are valuable-we should go far enough in the direction proposed to enable us to get the real results? My hon. friend has stated that in former times great numbers of people went from Ontario and also from the maritime provinces to the United States. The platform orator on the Liberal side says that all this is stopped, and that the stream is now coming from the United States towards this side. But that, it appears from the figures the United States are publishing is a misrepresentation, and when we subtract one figure from the other there is very little difference between the streams; the reciprocity in population which my hon. friend talks about, seems to be about on an equal basis. I think, therefore, the minister should get his statistical branch an order so as to be able to keep account of the population going out and the sources from which it goes, as well as keeping a similar account of the population that comes in. For it would be a great advantage, if a certain stream was going, for instance, from Quebec, or from any other part of Canada, to inquire into the cause for this movement of population. Knowing the reason, and desiring our country to increase in population, not only the Dominion statesman, but the provincial statesman as well, will have a basis for their policies and can plan their work with a view to offseting the movement of the people from our country. Certainly, as it looks, now, it is impossible for us to say whether we are gaining in population as between ourselves and the United States. Certainly, as it looks to me, it is impossible for us to say whether we are gaining much as between ourselves and the United States.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I do not quite agree with my hon. friend that our statistics are less valuable and reliable than the Ameri-

can statistics. I think we have very good statistics.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: What I intended to say was that our statistics, -what we have of them, may be very good; still we are away behind in statistical work as compared with the United States. That has been clearly shown within the last two months.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I wish to correct the impression my hon. friend has given to the House. We have no statistical branch in our department. The work of our agents is either to induce immigration or to facilitate immigration, and the statistics we gather are merely an incident. The United States, on the other hand, has a statistical branch for the purpose of gathering statistics. We are prepared to establish a statistical branch if parliament orders it. But we have not been authorized to do so, we have not the money to establish it, and we can only get the information such as my hon. friend suggests when parliament gives us the money for that purpose.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the United States has a distinct statistical branch?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: They have a very much more elaborate service than we have, and the collection of statistics is an important feature of their service. The collection of statistics is a serious part of their immigration service, whereas it is merely incidental in ours.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The figures quoted by the leader of the opposition did not seem to us as if they could be correct.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Rather unexpected.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I think so. I do not know what other statistics we could get, or how they might be collected. But you can approximate. If their method is to count every one that goes into their country, of course you get a very large number.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
If the minister will look at the United States immigration report of a year ago, he will obtain full information as to just how they make it up. There were seven classes I think last year, and in making the calculation I did at that time, I omitted three or four of those classes as not properly coming within the general principle of immigration from one country to the other. But taking the four remaining classes last year, I think about
67,000	of actual immigrants went from Canada to the United States. I merely desired to say that full information is given in that report as to the methods they use, and
the principles they have adopted in compiling these statistics.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: This question was up a number of years ago when I was on the Agricultural Committee, and then we found great difficulty in reconciling the statistics of the two countries. We had our reports, of so many coming into Canada and so many going out; and actually those reports showed that not only had we lost every immigrant that came into Canada, but we had lost a lot of our actual increase as well. I merely wish to say to the leader of the opposition that if they connect with this statement he has read any account of settlers' effects, it will not prove anything conclusively, because settlers coming to us from the United States might bring with them a larger quantity of effects, and they might be worth a great deal more than effects going from our country into the United States. Now we have the value of household effects returned in our exports going to the United States. These export entries are made by parties who are leaving our country, we collect from the customs the export entries made by the men who are leaving the country. These are declared by the parties going away, and they are supervised by our officers. I only give this as a kind of a rough test to show that there must be some difference in the way the figures are collected in the two countries as read by the leader of the opposition.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Is there a record kept of settlers' effects exported?

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Yes. I say the figures are not conclusive with reference to the number of individuals, but they must be of value as showing that there is a much larger proportion of immigrants from the United States into Canada than from Canada into the United States. For instance, last year, of household effects, there was entered by parties leaving Canada to go to the United States, $2,076,137; while the value of settlers' effects entered as coming from the United States into Canada was $7,613,553, nearly four times as many. Now I say the figures read by the hon. gentleman are not conclusive because they may be varied by circumstances. I cannot think myself that there is anything like the proportion of people leaving Canada to reside permanently in the United States that there is of people coming in from the United States to reside permanently in Canada.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I have reason to know that the methods of classification to [DOT]the south of us are very different from those adopted on this side of the line. It is no uise for any one to say that there are not people going from Canada into

the United States to reside permanently, as there have been for years. The restlessness of our people would perhaps be one reason. However, whatever the reason may be, there is at times a movement towards the United States. It must be borne in mind that at certain seasons of the year there is a stream of emigration particularly from the maritime provinces, to the other side of the line, and recognized by our people as a movement into the United States, men going temporarily to engage in various occupations. From my own county I know that every spring a good many people, particularly from among the French Acadians, go over into Massachusetts and other New England states to work in the quarries, to engage in farming operations, while they leave their families at home. There are others who go early in the spring to engage with the Gloucester fishermen. They go from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, and during a certain season of the year they are engaged in fishing on board the American ships and sailing under the American flag. They then return. There is an annual stream returning every autumn. Many men who become involved financially in connection with their property go away, engage in certain occupations, make some money, come back and pay off their debts. This fact is perhaps within the knowledge of every member from the eastern provinces and from the province of Quebec. In the fall the men who go from our northern counties in New Brunswick to the state tof Maine to engage in lumbering operations can be counted by the thousands. But, they return in the spring. Under the methods pursued by the United States authorities, those whom I have named are classified as immigrants into the United States. Necessarily there must be discrepancies between any record which we may have, or any estimate which we may make, and their record of this incoming and outgoing population. There are unquestionably some who permanently leave the maritime provinces and settle in the United States. That must be so because I believe there are perhaps more Nova Scotians in Boston than there are in the whole city of Halifax. But that has been going on for years and there is this movement back and forth, which is temporary in its nature but which is calculated to mislead.

emigrants from the United' States when they return to Canada in the autumn? I am speaking altogether of the United States classification.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I can speak from personal knowledge with respect to that. The movements from the maritime provinces towards the United States are either over the Maine Central railway or by the steamship lines leaving St. John, Yarmouth, or Halifax. The American authorities take a minute record of every one who goes in through any of these channels. I know, as a matter of fact, that in going, particular inquiry is made of each passenger, of every one who may be on board the train or on board the steamer, but on returning, when they leave Boston or Portland or any of those ports, a record is not taken of those who come back into the maritime provinces. I know that for a fact, and I think it explains in a great measure many of the difficulties that present themselves in thinking out the question or in attempting to reconcile the apparent differences. I can quite appreciate what my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), has said. We are led to believe that there are a great many coming into Canada, or at least that there have been during the last few years. If it were true that there were those leaving our shores, in great numbers to settle in the United States we might well pause to inquire just what is the net gain that we are making. It would be a very desirable thing, I am sure, to have this record if one could be accurately secured, but it becomes a question of the expense and of the ultimate value of such a record.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
While I in no manner at all challenge the honesty of the statistics of the United States in regard to the exodus of Canadians to the United States, the older members of the House remember, and are fully aware that the accuracy of those statistics was more than once challenged on the floor of this House. Some twenty years ago or thereabouts, the subject of the exodus of Canadians to the United States was one of constant debate in this House. The numbers of Canadians who were then going to the United States was very large, undoubtedly. But I remember distinctly that on a certain oc-

casion-and I am sure that if my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) taxes his memory, he "will remember it also-that Mr. John Henry Pope-I just forget the year exactly, but it was about twenty years ago, when he was either Minister of Agriculture or Minister of the Interior-had a special inquiry made into this subject of the exodus from the province of Ontario to the western states. At the beginning of a session, when the matter was again brought up, he gave the result of his inquiry and it was shown that the statistics which were given by the American authorities-I will not say were not reliable -but were altogether contradicted by the inquiry which was made under the authority of Mr. Pope. If I had the time I am sure I could lay my hands upon this volume of ' Hansard,' although I am quite sure that my memory is absolutely accurate in regard to my statement of what occurred on that occasion.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I think the question the House has been discussing for a short time, introduced by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), is a very important one. I remember that last year when my hon. friend the leader of the opposition directed the attention of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) to this important question, ha startled the House, and, I think caused some surprise among Canadians in every part of Canada. For the last ten years we have heard a great deal of discussion in this House with respect to the large number of people who are pouring into Canada, and during the last four or five years we have had special emphasis placed upon the fact that a very large number of people are leaving the United States and coming into Canada to pursue their agricultural interests. I take that to mean that the agricultural interests of Canada are in a very much better condition than the agricultural interests of the United States. We have been told in this House from time to time that there is practically no class of people leaving Canada, and going to the United States now. In listening to the discussion the other day I noticed that the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Hunt) said in his speech:
A great many young people in my country are selling the old homesteads and moving across the line.
I suppose then we are to take it, Mr. Speaker, that there are a good many young Canadians leaving Canada still. When I have read the statistics showing the large number of people coming into Canada from the United States I have wondered that this was not a greater cause of alarm to the American people. I was very much surprised that the newspapers in the United
States, Congress, the Senate and leading men generally, have not taken up this question more earnestly than they have. The answer, I suppose, is in the figures which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has presented to the House. They are in a position to know whether they are getting in a sufficient number of people to offset the exodus. The Commissioner of Immigration has been questioned before the Agricultural committee with regard to this matter, and his answer always is that it is practically impossible to keep any record of the large number of Canadians that are going to the United States, but the Minister of the Interior now tells us this can be done if it were not for the expense. In my opinion a reasonable sum of money would be well expended to ascertain actually whether we are the gainers or the losers. Year after year parliament is being misled if the figures given by the leader of the opposition are approximately correct, and I think they are. The Minister of the Interier must no longer delay a thorough investigation into this matter, and if his department requires a small statistical branch for that purpose, parliament would willingly vote the money. After every census we are disappointed at the showing, even though we know a great number of people have come into Canada during the previous ten years, and I have no doubt this is due to the fact that while it is true we are gathering from the United States, it is also true that we are sending in return some of our best people. The Minister of the Interior and the Prime Minister himself should take into consideration the providing of means to ascertain how many Canadians are leaving our shores and going to the United States, so that a remedy may be applied.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
When we were discussing the vote for immigration this question was discussed by members on this side of the House, and I think we demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Minister of the Interior that there should be proper means taken to discover how many Canadians go to the United States year after year. Years ago the Liberals reproached the Conservative party because so many Canadians, and especially those from the maritime provinces, left Canada for the United States, but I believe that the same conditions prevail to-day, and probably in a more intensified form. I understood the Minister of the Interior to tell us when discussing the estimates that he thought the present statistics were unreliable and that steps should be taken to ascertain the real facts, but he seems to have forgotten that promise. The figures given by the Minister of Customs are likely to be explained by the fact that the Canadians who are going to the United States, especially from

the maritime provinces, are young men and young women, the 'best of our land, while those who are coming from the United States to Canada come largely to the three western provinces and are farmers who bring with them their implements and their horses and cattle. As they can buy horses in the United States more cheaply than they can in Canada-a point which bears upon the reciprocity agreement -they bring their horses across the line with them and their cattle too. If we had proper statistics prepared I believe it would be found that as many or probably more of the young people of the maritime provinces are going to the United States than ever before. This is greatly to be deplored because we have lots of room for them in the west, and we want them there.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I have no brief to speak for the United States immigration officials or the statistics which they present from year to year, and while I am prepared to believe the statement of the right hon. gentleman that some years ago the statistics were not reliable, yet I believe that the influx of vast numbers of Southern Europeans into that country made it necessary that the authorities should take cognizance of that condition and present the fullest information to the public regarding the character of the immigration, so that to-day I regard their statistics very complete. I am not so much concerned about the completeness of statistics merely to record the movement of people. Immigration is the most important question the people of Canada have to deal with because it means the very lifeblood of the nation. The minister has said that if parliament wishes for fuller statistics he is willing to make the arrangements, and to see that they are secured. In my opinion it is absolutely in the interests of the country that he should take such a course at once. If Canada is the great nation we believe it to be, and if we are going to have vast masses of people pouring into our country, it is in the interest of all the nation that figures should be placed before us representing the exact character of that immigration. In the statistics presented to parliament now we are told of a certain' number of United States' citizens coming to Canada. We know that the greater portion of citizens are created in the United States just as they are in Canada, that is through immigration. I, therefore, think that the country of origin should be specified. A citizen from some part of southern Europe goes into the United States, stays there a few years and becomes a citizen of that country. Then if he enters Canada we should have information of the race from which that citizen sprung, in other words the immigration from the United States should state if native born, and if not. from Mr. SCHAFFNER.
whence they originally came. I think it is absolutely necessary that we should have fuller statistics so that the people throughout the country can study these ethnological questions.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
It is patent that the ministers have shown that their statistics are no good, that they have no statistics of any real value, and I do not think anything has been said by any of them to disprove or cast any doubt on the American statistics brought forward by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden). The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) when he rose first, started to say that our statistics were good statistics, but the Minister of the Interior was too quick for him, he rose to interrupt him to prevent him saying something he would be sorry for. He promptly told him that these statistics of the Interior Department were only an incident, that he had no officers to get statistics, and when the Minister of Customs rose afterwards, he did not tell us that the statistics of the Canadian government were good, he had found out that he was mistaken, and was prevented from making a bad mis-'stafiementi. This merely confirms whati was said the other day in a debate regarding statistics about the reciprocity treaty. We then found that this government had no statistics regarding prices, that they never tried to get any, that the American government had plenty of statistics which they have published, and seem to have at their fingers ends. All the information the ministers had was what our good friends on the other side were kind enough to give them.
The Minister of Customs says that this question has come up many times, that he remembers some years ago when he was on the Committee on Agriculture discussing this matter, and he found the statistics very difficult to understand. He said that it sometimes appeared from the figures as if all our immigrants had gone to the United States, and in fact sometimes even part of our natural increase. The member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) has partially explained this, but to my mind there is another explanation. I think that many people from Europe who come into Canada nominally as immigrants to this country really come here for the purpose of going to the United States. They are counted as immigrants coming into Canada; our friends the government pass great numbers of them, and when they enter the United States they are counted as immigrants going to the United States. We probably all know of our own knowledge that immigrants have come into Canada and stayed here a short time, merely for the purpose of going to the United States. Why do they come here first? They come here on account of our extraordinary system

of bonusing immigrants and also on account of the fact that the United States is much more careful in the inspection of immigrants arriving in their ocean ports, New York and Boston, than of immigrants entering from Canada at border points. The Minister of Customs has given some figures with regard to settlers' effects which the member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) has explained very well. I do not see that these figures disprove the immigration figures which have been quoted from the United States authorities. It is true that many of the immigrants coming into Canada from Europe afterwards go to the United States, and it is quite evident that they will not have, per head, anything like the amount of settlers' effects that the people will who are coming from the western states into Canada, who have been farmers for many years, and who are bringing over all their personal effects. So I do not see that the dollars worth of settlers' effects quoted by the Minister of Customs disprove in any way the statistics which the United States government has provided on this subject. So long as the ministers of the Crown in this House have to admit that they do not know anything about our statistics, that they have no proof whatever that they are of any particular value, just so long they must abide by and agree to these statistics provided by the United States.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: The leader of the opposition did not attach much importance to them apparently.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I said nothing of that kind.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: You doubted them.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: No, I did not seek to challenge them at all. I asked whether or not their accuracy was challenged by this government, or accepted by them. So far as I know the Immigration Department of the United States government is as well organized a department as exists in the world, and I say that after having made some personal investigation of it, because I went to Montreal on one occasion, and spent two days in examining their methods. I am bound to say that any man who takes that trouble to understand their system will be convinced of the truth of what I have said. I would not for a moment cast a doubt on the accuracy of their statistics, but I do not know the principle on which they frame them. I repeat that the results set forth in their Teport of last year, and of this year were absolutely surprising to me, but that does not mean that I am challenging the accuracy of their statistics. I would be very sorry to do it.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) says the Americans count every person going into the United States. That is what our officers do with every person coming into Canada. If a man from the United States comes into Canada wishing to buy land, he is counted as an immigrant. We find that last year
103.000	came into western Canada, but if you look up the records to see how many took up homesteads, you will see that only
14.000	did so. A great many of these others who came into western Canada simply inspected lands, looked into the conditions there, and if they were not satisfactory, went back without buying, and a great many bought land, and returned to the south.
I rose principally to protest against the immigration of negroes into western Canada. We, with British Columbia, wish to see a white west. We do not wish that kind of immigrants coming into western Canada, and I wish to protest very strongly against this government allowing them to enter western Canada.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I would like to suggest that we do not meet here another year to discuss this question of immigration and have the Minister of the Interior or the Minister of Customs, ignorant as to whether the same basis of counting is used on the United States side and on the Canadian side. Any clever man, in either of these offices, could go over to the United States and analyse that matter, in company with the officers there, and find out exactly what the differences are, if any. My own opinion is that there is some difference; how far it goes we do not know; but I think it is the first duty of the government to eliminate that lack of information and get to the foundation of fact in reference to it.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
It affords me a great deal of pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to realize that the ministry realize their absolute incompetence as compared with the American administration with regard to this item of immigration. For years there have been hundreds of thousands of Americans coming into the Canadian west, and they 1 are among the shrewdest of the farming community from the different states. They have come to better their conditions. For years they have had this ninety millions of population to sell their products to; but they have realized that their condition would be better in Canada under the protection that we have had here in the past. They leave the United States and come to Canada with two or three carloads of stuff. When they leave their own states their horses are worth only $108 a head; when they land them in Canada they are worth $130, $140, or $150. Their milch cows which are worth only $40 a head in the states, are worth $48 when they are

landed in Canada. It is the same with their swine, their sheep and any other live stock they have. I do not refer to the conditions that may prevail if my right hon. friend carries through the reciprocity agreement which he proposes, and which we do not propose he shall. These people are wise people; they have been trying to make a livelihood on the other side and have not been successful, and they realize that in Canada they can be successful owing to the protection that they have in this country. They do not want the ninety-million market; they want the market that we have in this country, with the protection that prevails. That is the reason they have been coming here in hundreds of thousands. For that reason, and that reason alone, I would submit tc the First Minister that he had better revise his judgment with regard to the farmers of the west and reciprocity. One other matter I wish to refer to, and that is what my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe), has said with regard to the negro immigration into the Canadian west. It is a question that no man in politics desires to touch, for many reasons, but it is a question that every man in Canada in his heart thinks over. It is a great big question on the other side of the line, and we on this side should do everything in our power to keep it there, because it is a question which, in the minds of many of the deep thinkers of the United States, is going to be one of primest importance to the standing of that country inside of a very few years. It is a matter of the gravest importance, and one that is almost beyond the pale of parliament to discuss-not because it is not worth discussing, but because it is of such great importance that it should be discussed absolutely outside of partisan lines and only in the interest of Canada. It is a matter that I do not wish to touch, and that I would not have referred to had it not been referred to by my hon. friend from Lisgar. I almost regret that it has ever been brought up, not only on this occasion, but on other occasions, because the people of that race have a standing in Canada, and have shown their worth, and we can only judge of their failings as a people by what has occurred in the south. For that reason I do not wish to discuss the question here. I would caution the Minister of the Interior with regard to bringing people into Canada from southern Europe. While we on this side of the House approve of all northern European immigration, we absolutely disapprove of a certain class of southern European immigration as detrimental to the west; and when I say that I have only to quote his own words uttered in this House with regard' to the Mr. CAMPBELL
Galician immigration. The bread he cast upon the waters at that time will come back to him bearing fruit in as many folds as he likes.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: One matter to which I think the government should pay a little attention, is the special concessions which an immigrant from the south receives from the various railway companies. A man from across the border gets from them a rate of a cent a mile to any part of the west, while a good Canadian who wishes to make the same trip has to pay the regular rate. Now, that is an unfairness to our Canadians. The same would apply to young men who are coming from the maritime provinces. If they wish to come to the west they have to pay the usual rate, unless they can come on a home-seekers excursion such as occasionally takes place, but, of course, it is not convenient for all to come just when a home-seekers' excursion is leaving. So, this is a clear injustice to the Canadian home-seeker who wishes to locate a homestead in the western provinces. The minister should look into this and see to it that our good Canadians at least are given the same consideration as is given to those who come from across the line.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext: As this is a new matter, I desire to say a word at once with regard to it. It is a matter which has engaged the attention of the department. We have discussed it with the railway companies,- and,of course, so far as we are concerned, it is in the control of the railway companies absolutely. We have not been able to induce them to do differently from what they have been doing. They have business reasons of their own for the policy they pursue. The alternative appears to be that if attempt were made to press upon them to give the same conditions to our own people as they give to people from the United States, they would simply withdraw the concessions they give to people from the United States.

subtopic: EMIGRATION FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
This subject of immigration is one of great interest, but in the discussion of the last hour and a ha'.f it has been one of great disappointment also. I have never given great attention 'to (the study of immigration statistics, but, reading newspaper reports, and listening to the statements of the Minister of the Interior, I have been lead for years to believe that we were gaining, through our immigration system, very large additions to our population, and very considerably so from the United States-at a cost to us of a good deal of money. The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) has thrown some light on that matter this afternoon. He has taken the settlers' effects as a

guide. He read from the Trade and Navigation returns showing that last year's settlers' effects from the United States to Canada amounted to $7,613,500, and that settlers' effects from Canada to the United States amounted to $2,076,000. I can well understand the large amount of settlers' effects from the United States into Canada, because the arrivals from the United States in our western provinces almost always carry large quantities of farm machinery, horses, cattle, wagons, &c. But, to my mind, the Minister of Customs may be a litt'le out of the way when he makes the value of settlers' effects the basis of a comparison showing the number of people coming into and going out of the country. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) spoke of the migration from the maritime provinces to the United States. From the character of that migration, I should suppose the people going from the maritime provinces had taken very litt'le with them, whereas the people going into the western provinces from the United States bring a great deal. I think it would not be too much to say that the value of the settlers' effects coming into Canada would be three times as much for the average individual as the value of settler's effects carried by the people from the maritime provinces going into the United States. That may be even a little under the mark. If, for the sake of the comparison, we say that the people coming from the United States into our west bring $3.50 in settlers' effects for every $1 that is taken out by our people going from the maritime provinces to the United States, we find that practically we have an equal movement of emigration and immigration. I am a little afraid that that is really the case,-that we are losing just as much as we are gaining. We shall have to await the census returns to see if that can be verified or not. But it does look as though, while the minister is spending a great deal of money and filling up the western country at what we might ca'll the bung-hole, he is neglecting to see how much is running out of the spout from the maritime provinces. From what has been said this afternoon, I am very much afraid that our net gain is very little. I hope the Minister of the Interior will, even if it costs more, carry out some system of keep-" ing track of the people that go out of the country. It cannot be expected that this is to be done without money; but I am not aware that this parliament ever refuses any reasonable appropriation for any purpose of correct and useful statistics. The subject is so interesting and important, that I am sure parliament would gladly provide the money. I was much surprised to learn that no real account is kept of the people going out of the country as well 257
as those coming in. The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) referred to what had occurred about twenty years ago and what was said on the matter. We a'll remember the howl of Sir Richard Cartwright, particularly with regard to the exodus. He magnified it to such an extent that I believe he got away beyond the bounds. He talked about the people we were losing and about there being a million native born Canadians in the United States at that time. I do not know whether he got his figures from the American returns or not, but I always thought he magnified them, and magnified them for a purpose. He did it to show that the National Policy had failed. And we have the National Policy to-day, with what hon. gentlemen opposite say are improvements made in it by themselves, yet the population seems to be going out of the country as fast as it was then. I merely rise to voice my opinion in favour of the Minister of the Interior taking steps to get for the future more correct statistics than he has been getting with regard to the people leaving the country.
It would be just as interesting to us to know whether we are losing population as to know whether we are gaining it. My opinion is that we are lbsing about as much as we are getting, so far as the United States are concerned. No doubt the figures furnished us by the Department of the Interior axe fairly correct of the number of people coming in from Great Britain and European countries. We are not losing people going across the water. I trust the minister will take the necessary steps to inform us in the future as to the movement of population both ways, not only from the United States into Canada, but from Canada into the United States.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, the circumstances surrounding this reciprocical convention are somewhat special and very interesting. First, the measure came to us in a very sudden and unexpected manner, as is the government wanted to bring upon parliament and the country a bunch of surprises, as if their intention had been to cause us a surprise. In 1910, it was the War Navy ; in 1911, it is the reciprocity. But not a word had been said during the general election of 1908 of these most vital and serious questions. At the very first session, thanks to the German scare, a ghost sprung for a purpose, we are launched at full steam in the military imperialism, and, in 1910, the German scare being over, the



government .gave us this famous navy, Canadian at time of peace, British at time of war. In order that the people, especially of the province of Quebec and of the West, should forget the navy, and to distract public opinion, the government brings up the reciprocity.
When the general elections of 1908 were over, and there was no fear of the electorate we went full Sail into naval militarism. In 1911 after the famous election of Drummond-Arthabaska, when the salutary fear of the voter began to tell upon the government, they try on something to show that they want to kill commercial imperialism itself. What then of the argument brought during the election of Drummond-Arthabaska, that the government was creating a navy in order to protect our oceanic trade. One more contradiction dont count much with our hon. friends opposite, principally when the cup is full.
Where are those who in Canada, in these last years, ask this reciprocity with our neighbours? The great national policy has caused in this country a great many struggles. Inaugurated in 1878 by Sir John A. Macdonald, modified in 1897, but maintained in principle by this government, as we have been told by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton), who knows pretty well, because he, along with his collegues at that time, the hon. Minister of Finance took part in this tariff reform ; this national policy, as I said, had been definitively accepted by the two parties and was giving satisfaction to the Canadian people. New cities were springing up everywhere like magic and existing cities were doubling their population.
