speechtext:
(Translation.) I say since both parties have agreed to put in . force a policy of protection, of moderate protection, it is true, but at any rate a policy of protection. That policy 'has developed the local market, surely the most profitable for us, and that market, supplemented by 4he interprovincial trade, takes up almost all of our natural products, that is to say, about 80 or 85 per cent, for local consumption. So that there remains only about 15 or 20 per cent of our surplus production which is sent over to Great Britain through our improved system of transportation which has cost us a great deal of money, and to the United States despite the walls put up by themselves, for they are absolutely in need of some of our products as raw material to feed their industries, for instance, wood for the manufacture of paper, and our hard wheat for their flour mills, stuffs which they are so badly in need of that they would have gladly Mr. NANTEL	*	! 4 ?
taken them from us, with or w'ithout reciprocity.
Who are they then who are Clamouring for this arrangement? You may be sure it was not the manufacturers, or the farmers of Quebec or of Ontario, still less the fruit growers and gardeners. The fruit growers have insisted that there should not be any change in the tariff. The opinion of manufacturers regarding this arrangement is known. Who then rvas asking for it? The grain growers in the west alone complained. With, as appetizers, the speeches made by the right hon. gentleman the Prime Minister during his trip through the west last summer. They, to the exclusion of all others, asked that our fiscal laws be changed. To the children of the soil the answer was that they came too late. To the grain growers, born in foreign lands, and who only of late years joined the Canadian household, greetings of welcome were extended. Is that because they seem to be the wards of the financial nabob, of the railroad king, James J. Hill? Quite possible. Their demands have been in the main com plied with, and yet they are not satisfied. As a matter of fact, what they are after is unrestricted reciprocity. They are quite outspoken in the matter, adding that they will keep on fighting until they get what they are intent on obtaining. It is clear that these gentlemen have a great pull, and at the time of their visit to Ottawa during the winter, it was contended that they had come under the patronage of Hill, and even that the latter had paid their railway fares.
Now, who are these grain growers, and are they so very much to be pitied? Are they humble toilers of the soil, poor fellows who barely manage to eke out a living, like those who formerly in Quebec and Ontario cleared the bush, wielding at times the axe, and at times shouldering the gun to fight away the Iroquois? Not by any means; they are wealthy farmers who migrated from Dakota and elsewhere, and who, after selling their farms at advanced prices, settled in the Canadian west with a view to securing for themselves larger farms at the rate of $10 an acre.
While travelling through the west, during the autumn of 1909, I came across one of these pure-blooded Yankee grain growers in the vicinity of Calgary. I was in company with a lands agent who introduced me to that gentleman farmer. Instead of painfully cutting and turning over the furrow with the help of oxen, as described by the poet, he had recourse to a traction engine, and over his immense domain, everything was done by steam. He had come in the warm season to put in the grain; in the autumn he was to return to see to the threshing and to figure out his thousands

of bushels of grain before the wintry weather set in, then he would go down south to enjoy a milder climate, in the vicinity of Los Angeles, where he intended to spend the winter and make the most of life, which as he thought, was very short.
Of course, I do not mean to say that all grain growers are as wealthy as this man; but they are not the most to be pitied amongst Canadians. These grain growers should be treated fairly, and their just requirements complied with, in the same way as those of other members of the great Canadian family; but they should not expect us to subvert and disorganize the fiscal system which is found to be satisfactory to Canada.
The treaty of 1854, which remained in force until 1866, gave rise to discussions which lasted eight years. That famous fiscal arrangement which we are called upon to ratify to-day, has more importance than the treaty of 1854, for as a matter of fact, its scope is wider, and why then should we be expected to dispose of it in the space of a few months. We did not hear of this measure until after New Year's. Ratified in the United States by the House of Representatives, it is now before the Senate. As will be seen, matters are being pushed ahead rapidly. Evidently the grain growers who are the promoters of this move, patronized by Hill, who is interested in the passing of the Bill, have a great deal of pull.
The last person to take a "hand in promoting this fiscal measure, was Mr. Bryce, British ambassador at Washington. I shall quote from the ' Gazette ' of April 24, 1911, the following extract:
(Text).-Mr. Bryce, ambassador of Great Britain to the United States, has been at Detroit speaking in praise of the Canadian reciprocity arrangement. Lord Sackville, one of Mr. Bryce's predecessors at Washington, twenty-three years ago, was sent home for talking too much about United States political issues. The precedent was not a notably decent one, however, and may be barred by the statute of limitations as to such matters. And Mr. Bryce may be privileged.
(Translation.) As may be seen, great interests are involved in this question, and one might surmise that this reciprocity scheme originated in the minds of the President of the United States, and of the British Ambassador, Mr. Bryce, to favour the political aims of the president of the United States and of the Liberol party, as against the Unionist party in England. Must it be understood that the fate, the destiny of Canada is an incident, a side issue in the political warfare going on between the parties in those countries. The United States are in a state of unrest, there is a crisis impending, while here in Canada business is flourishing. Last autumn, in the United 2571
States elections were fought on the question of the cost of living. The Democratic party won out against the Republicans. A change of government is about to be affected; a reform is needed to remedy the present state of things, and the government which is about to come into power, is bound to apply that remedy which is the lowering of the tariff. So that, even should that arrangement not be ratified, there would be a change, and the best proof as to that is that, just now, in the United States Congress, they are discussing the free list, that is an enactment allowing the free entry of goods corresponding practically with that implied in this famous agreement. Consequently, it is likely that had we delayed, we might have obtained, without making any concessions ourselves, the advantages secured through this treaty.
In Canada, where everything is satisfactory, shall we, to help on our neighbours who need medicine, take the same medicine, though in perfect health? For the sake of our neighbours, shall we run the risk of contracting disease?
Now, this agreement is being made with a government about to fall from power. It is a foregone conclusion that before long, there will be a change of government, and as a consequence a change in the tariff, as the Democratic party are on the eve of taking hold of the government. In the meantime, we are going here to considerable pains in view of a state of things which is not at all likely to last very long, a state of things as problematical as a game of bluff, played by these parties in the United States to get hold of power.
An agreement has been gone into with a government which possibly may not be in a position to meet its obligations. True, the House of representatives has approved this agreement, but should the Senate reject it, it would mean to Canada a setback even more humiliating than those we have experienced in former times. Should not our plenipotentiaries have waited a little while and make sure that the government which was a party to this contract would be in a position to carry out their promises?
As I stated a moment ago, this famous question of reciprocity, as well as that concerning the navy, has never been submitted to the people at the general election of 1908. Have we a mandate to settle that reciprocity business? We have at most a general mandate, but no special mandate, since the question has never been submitted to the people. I know that parliament has the right to do anything it pleases. My professor in constitutional law taught that parliament was able to do anything except changing man into woman. Formerly, party leaders made known to the people, in a general election, their policy.

the important measures which they proposed to submit to parliament. It is no longer the fashion to-day. The high art consists in not revealing anything to the people, in going through an election in sphinx-like fashion, By-andnby, vital issues are submitted to parliament, as, for instance, the question of the navy and that of reciprocity; then supporters are whipped into line, the benefits of patronage are dangled before their eyes, and everything goes. Later on the electors are acquainted with what has been done, with the heavy expenditure incurred, and the disadvantages incident on a withdrawal from the position taken are emphasized. If the people approve of what has been done, so much the better; all is well that ends well. If the people withhold their approval, well, at any rate, the party will have enjoyed the exercise of power, four or five years in the meantime. That is a simple and practical device. If, in 1908, when, in his most touching tones, he appealed to his compatriots in Quebec, praying that they allow him to carry through his undertaking-the National Transcontinental railway-the Prime Minister had requested them besides to empower him to provide the country with a war navy and to conclude a treaty of reciprocity with the United States would the results have been the same? To say the least, we are justified in having our doubts as to that.
But this agreement is either good or bad. If it is really beneficial, why has it not been concluded for a given period, and why has it not been safeguarded against, put beyond party warfare and intrigue, especially on the other side of the frontier? The treaty of 1854 was passed for a period of ten years; otherwise, our neighbours would not have been long in denouncing it. Enlightened by past experience, our plenipotentiaries, if they were satisfied that they were making a good bargain with uncle Sam, should have laid down a fixed date, ten or twenty years, and thus secure to us the benefit of it for as long a period as possible.
Who then requested for either country the privilege of abrogating the treaty at will? Was it the representatives of the United States or those of Canada? That would be interesting information. Our plenipotentiaries, always careful to withhold from us information in this connection, have not told us about it. If such a clause was included at their request, they certainly blundered, since they were satisfied that the bargain was beneficial to us.
Stability is indispensable in tariff matters and treaties. The weak point in this arrangement is its unstable character. How should Canadians be expected to make preparations for taking advantage of that market, seeing that our neighbours are at liberty to shut them out at a moment's, notice?
Mr. NANTEL
The mere fact of our making the best of the opportunity offered might be sufficient reason in he eyes of our neighbours to deprive us of that market. It should be evident to all of us that the Americans, having abrogated the treaty of 1854 because they considered that, all things taken into account, we had the best of it, do not make this offer for our own sake. The fact that no definite period is indicated shows that our representatives themselves who concluded the arrangement did not have absolute confidence in that measure and accepted it as something doubtful, and rather risky as regards any benefits it might confer upon us. It is an experiment, implying some risk and uncertainty, and in exchange for that risky and uncertain prospect, we are asked to give up what we possess as a certainty. That fiscal arrangement is a medicine which our plenipotentiaries are desirous that 'Canada should take, though in good health, while they are themselves unable to give the assurance that the medicine will give good results, or even is perfectly safe. All they can say, 'is that should the medicine turn out to be noxious, we shall give up taking it.
Another grave defect of that agreement, consists in discriminating against certain classes of the people, refusing to some of them the protection which it ensures to others in such a way as to develop antagonism and cause friction, and that should make it short-lived, if ever it is fit to live. For instance, it refuses protection to the market gardener while it grants it to the grain-grower. Every one knows that tfiere is a great deal of capital invested in market gardening. Market gardeners are actually manufacturers, but this agreement withdraws all protection from them.
However, it is stated that a market of one hundred millions is going to be opened to us. That is all very fine, but it should not be lost sight of that the Americans are a people of producers and exporters of products similar to ours, and on a larger scale than we are ourselves. Without referring to any statistics, I may state, relying on those previously supplied, that the United States are about the country which exports the largest quantities of products similar to those we produce ourselves. Moreover, this agreement opens our doors to twelve other countries against which we are protected for the present by our fiscal laws. True heretofore our trade intercourse with these twelve nations has not been very extensive, but who can foretell what extension such trade may not take when free entry to our market is given them?
The object of the Americans in showing such generosity in this trade arrangement, was to draw to their country our natural products, the raw material, such as nu!n wood, wood pulp and our hard wheat, which they cannot do without. Under that trade.

arrangement, we are running great risk of injuring our local market and interprovincial trade.
For instance, who does not realize to-day the importance of our local market? There is no need of statistics for that object; it is enough to be a consumer, to supply oneself on the Montreal market or elsewhere, to know that the prices which farmers sell at to-day are exorbitant and have reached their top limit. It is not within the memory of a man that from $13 to $15 has been paid for a hundred pounds of pork, $12 for a hundred pounds of beef. ~ The prices of these products could not therefore be higher. If, under this arrangement, it is hoped that such prices will be further increased, then woe to the workingmen and consumers in the cities.
On the other hand, the farmer may suffer from a fall in prices though the competition of products from the Argentine, which is one of the countries to which we give free entry under this arrangement, and which through the conservation of meats in cold storage compartments, will be in a position to cater to our markets, with the result that our farmers may be obliged to sell their own products a little cheaper. To this our opponents answer that the agreement under consideration will have the effect of enabling our farmers to get higher prices, while consumers will get commodities cheaper. These two contentions are difficult of agreement. If sane reasoning cannot show the absurdity of such a stand, it will of itself fall to the ground. If the farmer gets a higher price, surely it must be that the consumer is made to pay that higher price. Nowadays production is very costly, because labour is expensive. Farm help is very dear just now, and there is no means of extending farm operations unless there be more help available.
A few days ago, the hon. member for Montcalm (Mr. Rafortune), while acknowledging that this agreement might interfere with certain occupations, such as that of the market gardeners, contended that the latter, might alter their system of farming and grow hay, for instance, in accordance with the new system advocated in this House; that of the continous growing of hay on the same land.
But those good people who formerly accepted literally the teachings of the Minister of Agriculture surrounded by his agricultural lecturers, and who, in accordance with such teaching, devoted their whole attention and energy to market gardening or to dairying, would be obliged to alter their convictions and accept the agronomic heresies of that same Minister of Agriculture who has become a political partisan; all this in spite of the opinion of the specialist; Professor Robertson, of
MacDonald College, who declares that fifty million dollars' worth of butter exhaust the soil less than one thousand tons of hay worth $14,000. Really, our farmers will be very much perplexed if they understand that the American hay market may be taken from them at any moment, whereas they are always sure of selling at all times their fruit, vegetables, butter and cheese.
This agreement, moreover, is bound to disorganize and injure our transportation lines as between the different Canadian provinces, on one hand, and on the other in communicating with outlying countries, more especially with British possessions and even with the capital of the empire; it will become impossible to complete and improve such lines. In this respect the denunciation of the treaty of 1854, by which our neighbours intended to injure and annoy us, has proved a boon. Had that treaty continued in force, would we to-day have those railways and waterways which cross our territory in every direction? They have cost us much money, but we are proud of them, feeling as we do that they are our best asset. Would we then have made such gigantic progress in the building up of the Canadian nation? I say that we would not. Being deprived of the American market, which was then our only market, we were obliged to count upon ourselves alone. We have created our local and interprovincial markets; we have succeeded in reaching the British market, the most important in the world. There still remains for us much to do in that direction in the way of improving and perfecting our national organization. If the bulk of our produce, by reason of the new state of things that it is wished to establish, take a different direction from that which we have devised-perhaps somewhat in opposition to ordinary geographical rules -where will be, in future, the stimulant required to induce us to extend and improve those transportation lines. It is not plain that there will be none? What will become of the Georgian Bay canal and other works of a similar nature? If this agreement were ratified, the trend of trade instead of being east and west would be north and south; the direction would be changed and our product following the waterways of the great lakes would accumulate at St. Paul for the benefit of Americans and to the detriment of our own transportation.
Such a policy implies free trade in natural products and in certain manufactured articles. It is the first step towards absolute free trade in all products; it is a foretaste of free trade not only with the United States but with all countries. To establish and justify free trade in all products, it would be sufficient to resort to the same process and use the same

arguments which are set forth in support of the present agreement. It is, therefore, a return to the programme of unlimited reciprocity, the only difference being that it is reached by a more tortuous way. As a matter of expediency, now as in 1897, the principle of protection, is apparently maintained. But, in reality, as I have before stated, this agreement is but a disguised return to the free trade programme of 1891, a return to unlimited reciprocity. It is quite plain that not daring to make such a move openly it is sought to attain the same and toy indirect means. -
The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neeley) at a meeting of the faithful held at Ottawa, said:
The manufacturers are not hurt by this agreement, but they realize that once the people taste the sweets of freer trade in natural products, they will demand freer trade in manufactured goods as well.
For my part I believe in the policy of protection, especially in a young country possessing raw material and all the waterpower that can be desired; a country, moreover, surrounded by protected states. I cannot accept this agreement, which I consider wrong and dangerous for the country.
Protection saved France, and thanks to protection Germany is threatening Great Britain's commercial supremacy, and even causing the latter some anxiety as to her naval supremacy. I fear those free traders to whom free trade is as a religion. They ardently support the present measure in the hone that it is but the forerunner of a more complete surrender. I have quoted the member for Humtooldt. I might also quote the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith). In the course of the debate the hon. member for Red Deer, that paragon of free trade, that proud disciple of Cobden, gave full scope to his free trade ideas under the paternal eye of the hon. the Prime Minister, and as he spoke his chief seemed to drink in each one of his words as if they had sprung from the very fountain of youth. They seemed to make him twenty years younger and bring him back to the times of the 1891 campaign.
In support of this opinion, let me quote from a portion of the letter of Sir Charles Tupper to Mr. Fielding, which is published in to-day's issue of the Montreal 'Gazette,' the title of this article is 'Macdonald versus Laurier' and reads as follows:

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.

speechtext:
You say that Sir John A. Macdonald was in favour of reciprocity in 1891; but you do not explain that he was fighting a desperate battle to prevent Laurier and Cartwright, who were co-operating with Wiman and Far-rer-avowed annexationists-from carrying unrestricted reciprocity with the United Mr. NANTEL.
States, which involved Canada taking the tariff made at Washington, with its discrimination against Great Britain.
Have you forgotten that the Hon. Edward Blake left his party on the ground that that policy would end in annexation to the United States, which, at that important crisis, you supported? The policy for which Laurier and Cartwright and Wiman and Farrer were struggling.
It is true that in the struggle, which cost Sir John A. Macdonald his life, in maintaining British institutions for Canada, we succeeded. But before the election Mr. Laurier made the following solemn declaration:-
' I have read the history of unrestricted reciprocity in this way-that every reform has cost to the reformer years of labour, and those years of labour I, for one, am ready to give; and though the Democrats may be defeated in the States, and though Canadians may grow faint-hearted in Canada, the Liberal party, as long as I have anything to do with it, will remain true to the cause until that cause is successful. I will not expect to win in a day, but I am prepared to remain in the cool shades of opposition until the cause has triumphed, and you shall never hear a complaint from me. I tell you the Liberal party will never cease from the agitation until they triumph and obtain continental free trade. We are asked, sometimes, gentlemen, what is the programme of the Liberal party. This is the programme of the Liberal party, to obtain a continental freedom of trade. Success will certainly crown our efforts at no distant day. Fixing our eves steadily on the goal, we shall go on steadily until we reach it-unrestricted continental reciprocity.
Further in the same letter:
I am opposed to your agreement with the United States, because Mr. Bayard in 1888 assured Mr. Chamberlain and me that the policy of the Democratic party was to remove as soon as they were able the duties on all the articles in your agreement, and President Taft now sees that he oan only secure his re-election policy.
We owe nothing to the Republican party, and would, gain everything without any entangling alliance, which will, I fear, end in the destruction of British institutions in Canada.
You ventured to claim the prosperity of Canada as due to the Laurier government. You cannot deny that, without confederation and the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway, Canada could not have attained the great position that she has.
Further again:
Mr. Laurier (now 'Sir Wilfrid) pledged to tear up protection and triumph on its head and body, succeeded in obtaining power by a Janus-faced policy on the question of race and religion, but not until he had secretly assured the manufacturers that they would be safe in his hands, and then oalled you to his aid as Finance Minister, and you, having failed in your first effort, which I denounced, succeeded.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the House rose at six o'clock, I had laid down as a proposition that this commercial agreement was an earnest, a preparatory measure as it were or the coming back to free trade, and in support of this statement, I had quoted extracts from a letter of Sir Charles Tupper, that veteran of Canadian politics who 'in his 90th year, is by no means willing to allow hon. gentlemen opposite to misrepresent his statements. In support of this view, let me quote a few extracts from a speech delivered a few days ago in New York by the President of the United States; Mr. Taft.
The treaty provides for free trade in all agricultural products; and in rough lumber down to the point planning. It reduced the duties on secondary food products by a very substantial percentage and it makes such reductions on a number of manufactured articles that those engaged in making them have assured us that the reductions will substantially increase the already large Canadian demand for them.
And further on he adds;
We tendered to the Canadian commissioners absolute free trade in all products of either country, manufactured or natural, but the Canadian commissioners did not feel justified in going so far. It is only reasonable to infer, therefore, that with respect to these articles upon which they refused free trade to us, they felt that the profitable price at which they could be sold by our manufacturers in Canada was less than the price at which their manufacturers could afford to sell the same either to their own people or to us. Hence it follows that their refusal to agree to free trade in these articles as we proposed, is the strongest kind of evidence that if we should take off the existing duty from such articles coming into the United States it would not affect in the slightest degree the price at which these articles could be furnished to the public here. In other words, the proposition to put on the free list for entrance all articles that Canada has declined to make free in both countries would not lower the price to the consumer here.
And further on :
It is said that it injures the farmers. I deny it. It is strictly in accordance with the protective principle that we should only have a protective tariff between us and countries in which the conditions are so dissimilar as to make a difference in the cost of production.
The president then entered into an extended argument to prove that conditions of production in Canada were substantially the same as those in the United States. The difference, if any, was in favour of the United States as that had a greater variety of product cotton and corn, and hogs and cattle fed on corn were distinctly better crops in the United States than in Canada, he said, while
the difference as to wheat and barley and oats was the same in different parts of both countries
And further again ;
He realized he said that the agitation had raised opposition to the agreement. There was one way to clarify the situation, however, and that was to give the agreement a trial. If it were found that there was an injury to the farmers they possessed sufficient control by legislation to cause the ending the agreement, as neither country was hound to continue it indefinitely.
Finally ;
There are other natural resources which I need not stop to enumerate, which will become available to. us, as if our own, if we adopt and maintain commercial union with Canada, and this is one of the chief reasons that ought to commend the CanacUan agreement to the farseeing statesmanship of leaders of American public opinion.
It appears therefore, from this speech delivered by the president, that his intention is to promote free trade between the two countries, not only in natural but also in manufactured products. One of the motives of the agreement is to give Americans free access to our natural resources.
As I am now referring to this question of natural resources, I will remark that this agreement appeals so little to Canada, that the different provinces and more especially three of the most important ones, have adopted restrictive legislation to protect their natural resources.	_
Let me first mention the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, who have enacted special statutes to protect the export of timber to the United States. And since the present treaty is on its way-it is now being discussed by the United States Senate-New Brunswick has adopted a statute to protect the natural resources of that province against American invasion.
The hon. member for Red Deer, in his speech on this question, spoke enthusiastically of the condition of workmen in Great Britain. He intimated that notwithstanding free trade, British labour is the best paid in Europe.
A most singular fact! If wages are so high in England, why should there be in that country a constantly increasing army of unemployed, offering a most difficult problem for British statesmen? Why are there so many people idle? Why has it become necessary to have recourse to special legislation for the relief of the poor [DOT]by establishing the system of old age pensions? If free trade is useful in certain respects, it seems also to give rise to many drawbacks. Is not pauperism one of the curses of England? Is it not so serious a problem that statesmen have sought .to solve it by the statute voted on

the 1st August, 1908, and which in 19091910 costs the country two hundred and eighteen millions of francs and in 19101911 two hundred and thirty millions? Therefore, _ the advantages of free trade do not go without serious drawbacks. England, that predestinated country where free trade, like the River Pactolus, was going to bring prosperity, is also the country in which the government is most at a loss to find new sources of taxation to feed the ever growing budget.
Allow me to quote here a few lines from a very interesting book entitled * The English Crisis.'
Grave still is the downfall which threatens a nation where the people live almost exclusively in cities. It is impossible to travel through England without being struck with the contrast between the labouring masses in the cities and the peasants. Nothing can be more lamentable than the sight of the populace that assembles in Trafalgar Square in winter or that of the masses that fill the political meeting halls in the populous quarters of London; the men are nervous, pale and stunted, alcohol and tea have dissolved their muscles and made them an inferior race. A gulf growing deeper every day separates this populace from the prosperous and wealthy classes trained in the sports_ of the public schools, and also from the higher class of working men who enjoy leisure and play football. To find that impression of strength formerly resulting from contact with the Anglo-Saxon, one must travel through the rural districts. There, John Bull survives: the yeoman farmer appears, his pipe between his teeth, his (hands jin his pockets, his broad sole set flat on the ground, his self-satisfied smile showing his confidence in the strength of his fists and of his jaw. It is not surprising that the founder of the Physical Education and Progress League, Sir Lander Brunton, found in the abandonment of farms for the cities, in the drift to the urban centres the primary cause of the degeneracy of the English race.
Protection, properly applied, more than any other fiscal system is calculated to secure the necessary revenue for the development of our country and for the immense works which yet remain to be accomplished in a young country like Canada. We require a large revenue to complete our transportation lines and our national public works. If this agreement were ratified, the hon. the Finance Minister might be unpleasantly surprised when he came to make up his next budget speech.
He figured that the decrease in revenue would reach $2,500,000; hut I believe the amount should be doubled to cover the actual decrease. The more satisfactory arrangement is, the more will the revenue fall, and if we are anxious to carry on existing works or to start others, it.' will be necessary to get the necessary funds.
But it is contended that the arrangement does not concern manufacturers. There is Mr. NANTEL.
no need for discussing that point; it is perfectly well known to what extent manufacturers are effected: they themselves feel the blow aimed at them and the harm it has done. They are moving accordingly, and are eloquently demonstrating the falsity of that contention. They realize the position in which they have been put, and they have reason to be suspicious. The policy of protection, definitely accepted, in 1897, by both parties, gives satisfaction to all, and they are anxious that it should be maintained. An era of prosperity and a great swing of progress had been the result of its application, but this agreement upsets and turns everything up side down. It deprives us of all control over our tariff legislation, and puts us in many respects under the thumb of our neighbour. It does away with the principles laid down by the right hon. Prime Minister who declared on several occasions that there would be no further change or alteration of the tariff without the parties interested being notified in advance, and an investigation carried on by a commission of experts in connection with which all interests affected would be heard. This agreement does away with those principles and radically changes a large part of the tariff, without putting these people on their guard. If it has been possible to effect those changes, many others may be effected in the future.
I say that this agreement will make us utterly dependent on the Americans as regards our fiscal legislation. I see, for instance, among the articles included in the free list, separators and cream separators which were, it is true, on the free list under the statute, hut to which, at the next revision, it might have been possible to ensure legitimate protection. I contend that these apparatus should be protected, even should the only result be to prevent the importation into Canada of inferior makes which are. sent from all quarters. As long as this agreement remains in force, we cannot think of protecting that industry without the consent of our neighbours, otherwise the whole agreement falls to the ground.
Then again, that arrangement will prevent American industries requiring our raw material to settle down in Canada; they will build preferably within the territory of the United States. That is only natural; but it means a loss of capital to Canada.
Another objection to that treaty is that we are dealing with a people much stronger than ourselves. A people of one hundred millions against one of eight millions; it is a giant dealing with a dwarf. At the first difficulty which may arise, the dwarf will be overcome. Force overrides right very often. It is always unsafe for the weak to associate with the strong; the story of the iron pot travelling in company with the earthen pot should teach us a

lesson; at the first jar tire earthen pot goes to pieces. When Canada's population reaches the twenty-five or thirty million mark; when it has completed its system of transportation, and built the Georgian Bay canal, it may then be desirable for us to negotiate a treaty of commerce with the United States. But I believe that until we have reached that point of development, it would be highly imprudent to conclude such an arrangement with our neighbours.
Now, it is stated: this is a new market which is opened to us and we are not in any way deprived of our present markets. That is so, provided this treaty has not the effect of injuring our local market, for this new market can toe taken away from us at the very moment when we least expect it. The interprovincial trade is of great value to us, and as evidence I may point out that timothy seed-an article which the farmer cannot do without-is so scarce just now in Montreal that it is selling at $15 a hundred pounds. Why? Because, it appears, the seed sown last year has been shipped to the west to fill orders of the trade in that district. That gives an idea of the importance of the local and interprovincial trade. I believe that if we should lose that market, we would find no equivalent in the one which this arrangement proposes to secure to us.
In respect to loyalty, it is contended that our loyalty to the British flag should not be made dependent on the sale to the Americans of a few bushels of wheat or a few bales of hay, more or less. Quite right. On the other hand, fortunately, the future of Canadian trade, thanks to the energy of our Canadian statesmen, since the abrogation of the treaty of 1854, no longer depends on the sale of these few bushels of wheat or bales of hay to the Americans. Owing to the sacrifices we have made, to the great works we have carried through, we are independent from those who were intent on starving us in 1854. Why should we once more put ourselves at their mercy? We have secured to our products a goodly part of the British market, the best in the world; let us endeavour to retain it and develop it as much as we can.
Are there any who sincerely believe that if the treaty of 1854 had not been repealed, Canada would occupy a position as prominent as that it now occupies. I say no. Had not that treaty been denounced, we would have remained forever under the control of the Americans. That repeal was then beneficial to us. Why should we once more agree to being dictated to by the Americans?
Annexation has been referred to. I for one have no fear of wilful annexation, especially as long as tihere are in Canada French Canadians having a word to say
on the subject, for my fellow-citizens feel that they are fairly dealt with under the protection of the British flag, that their religion, their language and their institutions are secure under the constitution and that they enjoy greater safeguards in the folds of that flag than they likely would in the folds of the stars and stripes.
I am aware of all that,., but I am also aware that the most prominent of American statesmen who discussed the question of reciprocity in rather reckless fashion made a plea for annexation which should induce us to be careful, and which even statesmen in Germany have considered worth while discussing in their parliament.
I am also aware that several of our most prominent Canadians, whip are no longer in politics, have pointed to annexation as the inevitable outcome of it all. In any case, if there is no real danger of annexation, it must be admitted that the Americans have not been able to conceal their innermost thoughts in this connection.
However, a real danger is that of the seceding of some of the western provinces, especially if there be no closer control exercised over the character of the immigration going into that part of the country. Americans have been coming into Canada for several years back at the rate of 50,009 or 60,000 per year, on an average. Should those proposals be ratified will the result likely be to attract here a still larger number of Yankee settlors? It seems to me it will. I stated in 1909, on the floor of this House, that this immigration was not of the best and the most desirable type. I sav so once more.
Those American railways which have terminals in our country and make themselves at home in our country are another source of danger; they attract our trade as so many suction pumps, and take it to the other side of the line.
A striking fact is that the originator of the policy which is responsible for the two danger points implied in these proposals, the man who more than any other helped to bring them into existence, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton), has-seceded from his leader on this very question, and is fighting the government. It is unfortunate that he did not find his Damascus road at an earlier period.
It is contended that the markets which are open to us to-day will continue to be open to us in the future. Yes, provided they are not injured by the new impulse given to our trade in other directions. It is evident that should the bulk of our trade take the direction of the United States in direct line from north to south, along the various railway lines owned by James Hill, acting as so many suction pumps and drawing our wheat towards the

United States flour mills, our railway and steamship lines will be running empty and the companies w'ill soon be tired of carrying on an unprofitable business. It will be found more difficult to undo such a state of things than it would be to prevent its establishment. That is a grevious danger whidh these proposals will only tend to make worse, a danger to which we should not close our eyes.
The hon. Minister of Finance, speaking the other day at Montreal, said:
There is a distinct danger that the east and west may be brought into antagonism if not into open hostility.
Further on he added:
The west is going to dominate Canada and we who live in the east, if we are wise, may as well see that and look ahead.
What kind of west is it going to be? A wise prudent and sympathetic west, or a rash, reckless and dangerous west.
Yes, the west may turn out to be actually an element of danger, not only from the economic, 'but from the national point of view. Has not a movement in favour of secession been launched in former days in the maritime provinces for reasons of minor importance if compared with those existing in the west? And tihe hon. minister wonders what will be the complexion of the west. I say the west will be such as you make it. If you continue bringing into the west Americans by hundreds of thousands, and if you throw them in with other hundreds of thousands of people who have come from all parts of the world, booked at the rate of five dollars a head, a mixture of all nationalities, it is much to be feared that these Americans will remain Americans or will not easily be Canadianized. I think you will hasten and intensify the danger toy persisting in that Obnoxious immigration policy.
If the east is one day to toe controlled by the west, it is incumbent on us to defer and prevent as much as possible that danger, and with a view to making that state of things more bearable, immigration should be more closely scrutinized and a better selection made of those who are destined to rule over us. We should make it a point to direct towards the west settlers from the other provinces of the Dominion; for instance, from Quebec and Ontario, and also from the British Isles, instead of promoting the immigration of American settlers on our soil. If we are bound to be ruled by the west, let us keep an eye on those whom we admit into the country, as foreigners may make trouble for us.
In the midst of that medley of settlers of all nationalities who take up lands in the west, the Yankees who are educated, wilv and ambitious, will in the end secure Mr. NANTEL.
the leadership. Canadianization w'ill progress slowly and may never be accomplished thoroughly and satisfactorily. The stars and stripes will be unfurled as often as the national emblem.
If you give to all these people the advantage of trading more freely with the corresponding States of the Union, than with the Canadian provinces, it is not necessary to peep very far into the future to detect the danger that is awaiting us, to realize its full consequences.
If it is the ultimate destiny of the west to dominate in this country, let us make it our duty to send there only desirable settlers coming from the United Kingdom and from the older provinces of the Dominion. We must deal fairly with those who are there already, but there is no need to spoil them by undue favours the only effect of which would toe to give them wrong dispositions. Our aim should be to allure them towards Canada rather than direct them towards the United States.
Mr. Chairman, I will vote against this agreement because I see in it more dangers than real advantages; because the prosperous state of affairs in this country is so general that we are not at liberty to run such risks; because it is desirable, in my opinion, to see the great bulk of our trade to continue by the routes we have opened and maintained at the cost of tremendous sacrifices and energy; because I would rather see the bulk of our commercial transactions done with the people of England than with the people of United States, who at a time that we were in great need of them, have wantonly closed their doors against us, and have put us in the necessity of seeking an outlet for our overproduction upon the English market; because I am satisfied that we will fare better with England than with the United States; because we can always expect fair play from John Bull if we know enough to resist his encroachments, while Uncle Sam might be found wanting in a moment of need. Above all I will vote against this agreement because the electors have not been consulted and have had no occasion to decide upon the advisability of this new policy, no more than upon the naval policy. I consider it a wrong principal not to .consult the electorate beforehand upon such important questions, and to appeal to the people afterwards and ask them to ratify what has been done.

Mr. Chairman, as I represent a constituency that for over 110 miles borders the United States, and one which is settled by 50,000 people, chiefly engaged in agriculture, I feel that I would not be doing justice to the people I represent, or to myself, did I not.

even at this late stage of the debate, express the views that I, and the great majority of my people hold upon this question. This is the most important question that has been presented to the consideration of the Canadian people since confederation. Every government in Canada has been in favour of reciprocity, and has done its best to make an agreement such as we have ot are about to accomplish now. I am not going to dwell particularly on what was the attitude of the Liberal party, forty, thirty or even ten years ago, and I am still less concerned as to what was the attitude of the Conservative party on this question during these past years. What we have to consider now, and what we have to decide is whether this agreement that has been arranged between the people of the United States and Canada is good for the peoiple of Canada to-day. If it is we ought to put it into force. If it is not we should not put it into force. That is the question that we have to decide in the very near future. We have had a good deal of opposition developed to this agreement, but it has been developed pretty much during the last three months. I remember very well that when my hon. Iriend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) read this agreement to the House hon. gentlemen opposite were surprised, they were pleased and they cheered the Finance Minister almost as much on that side of the House as we did on this.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: No, no.

speechtext: Why is all this change being made? Because since that time they have been whipped into line. Now, Mr. Chairman, it has been stated time and again in this House that we should not go on with this agreement because we have no mandate from the people of Canada. I have been through three Dominion elections and on the platform in these elections-

Well, if you can do it you are welcome, and I would be very glad to have my hon. friend across the way who has spoken come out, and try it. I was about to say that I have been through three Dominion elections, and on every one of these occasions I advocated reciprocity or better trade relations with the United States. But, I am not the only one to advocate reciprocity or better trade relations with the United States in the last election. My hon. friends opposite did the same thing in my constituency, let me tell you that, Mr. Chairman. The year before the elections, in the fall of 1907, the hon.
leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), made a tour through the west. He did me the honour of having a meeting in my constituency, at Weyburn-the only meeting he held in southern Saskatchewan -and at that meeting there was a gathering of the clans from east and west, brass bands in attendance, flags flying and everything lovely. In the evening they held a demonstration, and on the principal banner which was stretched across the skating rink were the words ' Reciprocity with the United States.' I am not going to try to make a point against the hon. leader of the opposition, because I do not suppose that he knew anything more about that declaration being put up there than I did. But, it shows that the Conservative party in the west, the year before the last election, which is exactly three and a half years ago now, were in favour of, and advocated reciprocity with the United States. One of the speakers at that meeting referred to the banner, and pointed out the advantages that would flow from a deal of that kind. So, when I say that not only the Liberal party, but the Conservative party have been in favour of that proposition I am stating the absolute facts of the case. It is no discredit to Sir John Macdonald that he did not get reciprocity. He tried his utmost to get it, and it was not his fault that he failed. The failure was due to the fact that the people of the United States at that time were not ready for reciprocity. It was not the fault of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that he did not get reciprocity when he went down to Washington not so very many years ago. Imagine, Mr. Chairman, if you can, the attitude^ of the hon. member for North Toronto if, this agreement that we have now before us being made available to us by the people of the United States, my right hon. friend the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) had refused to accept it? _ I can imagine him making this council chamber ring with the denunciation of the party that having an opportunity to get such an agreement for the people of Canada, and would hesitate to take advantage of it.
Let us see for a few minutes who are the people who are opposed to reciprocity. In the first place we have the Manufacturers' Association of Canada; in the second place we have some of the large financial institutions and some of the bankers; and in the third place we have the Conservative party in the House of Commons, not in the country, but in the House of Commons. Let us see to what extent these people are good judges

speechtext: What about the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton)?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not need to ask me about the hon. member for

Brandon. I admire and respect the hon. member for Brandon a great deal more than any member on that side of the House does, and if the hon. members on that side of the House had one-tenth of the political honour and honesty of the hon. member for Brandon it would not be three members, as we have on this side of the House who are not in favour of reciprocity, but it would be three dozen on the other side of the House who were in favour of reciprocity. Now, Mr. Chairman, let us see to what extent these people that I have mentioned-the Manufacturers' Association, the financial institutions and the Conservative party in the House of Commons- are good judges of what is good for Canada and what is not good for Canada. You will remember, and every member of this House will have it in mind, that fourteen or fifteen years ago, when the Fielding tariff was first brought in, in 1897, the Manufacturers' Association was up in arms, the financial institutions were up in arms and my hon. friends on the opposite side of the House were up in arms and denounced the Fielding tariff as a tariff that was going to ruin the country, wipe out our manufacturers and, in fact, was the worst piece of legislation that could be put upon the statute-books. Did anything of that kind come to pass? Has not the country continued to progress more and more ever since? The hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Nantel), who has just taken his seat, pointed out not five minutes ago that the country was so prosperous that we should not make any changes. The financial institutions took the same course and it turned out that they also were wrong and did not know what was good for Canada. My hon. friends in the House of Commons did the same thing and it turned out that they did not know what was good for Canada. Then, again, when the preference in favour of Great Britain was introduced, every one of these people opposed it in just the same way as being the worst possible that could happen in the interest of the people of Canada, and yet the results were such that even if my hon. friends opposite were in power to-morrow they would not dare lay their sacrilegious hands on that British preference although they opposed it tooth and nail. When this agreement comes into force, as come it will, and when it has been in force for six months, if such an unlikely thing could happen that hon. gentlemen opposite should come to this side of the House, they would no more change that agreement than they would dare change the preference to Great Britain.
I want to say a word or two, and I will be as moderate as I possibly can, to the manufacturers of Canada, and especially to the Manufacturers' Association. If the manufacturers have one great onemv in Canada, in my judgment it is not the Liberal party and it is not this government, but it Mr. TURRIFF.
is the Manufacturers' Association. The Manufacturers' Association have done more to put the people of Canada against the manufacturers than any other individual, or combination, or association could do. Last year, my right hon. friend toured throughout the west, met the farmers, heard their grievances and told them that he would take these matters into consideration. No sooner had he got home than the Manufacturers' Association got up a party to tour the west to counteract the effects that the meetings and delegations of farmers and grain growers might have on my right hon. friend. The result of that was to force the grain growers and farmers of the west to get up the big delegation that came down here last fall to interview the government and try to press home their arguments.
When the delegation from the west was in Ottawa I noticed that hon. gentlemen opposite were very anxious to show them around and to be gracious to them and to say what very fine fellows they were just then. Of course, the delegates were asking for something and these gentlemen opposite thought the government was not going to give it to them, and so they posed as friends of the farmers and the grain-growers. But since this agreement was put before the House which gives the farmers of the west-not all they had asked for in some respects it is true, but in other respects a great deal more than they had asked, and that they had ever expected to get-since then these gentlemen opposite cannot say too much against the Grain Growers' Grain Company which is part and parcel of the Grain Growers' Association of the three prairie provinces. Well, my friends in the west, the grain growers will know how to size up these gentlemen opposite pretty accurately. I want to point out to the manufacturers that this agreement does not hurt them to any extent, and I say further that if there is one class of people on this earth who should favour it and have nothing to say against it, it is the manufacturers of Canada, because, practically, they are left untouched. The result of this agreement will be that the people of Canada will be much more prosperous under it, and will make greater progress in the future than even in the past, in consequence of which there will be a larger market for the manufacturers of eastern Canada. Some people think that we in the west will become a manufacturing people, but personally I do not think so. I think it will always be cheaper to bring manufactured goods to the west than to transport the raw material and manufacture it there, because there is no question that the cost of living is higher in the west than it is in the east, and for many years to come we must be the consuming part of Canada, buying the bulk of the

goods that we use from the manufacturers of Ontario and Quebec. It stands to reason that the more people you have in the west and the more prosperous they are the more goods will the Canadian manufacturer sell. As has been pointed out by the Minister of Finance, there are now two million people in the west, and they consume more per capita than the people of other sections of the country because they earn more and they spend more, and inside of ten years it is safe to say that there will be five million people west of the Great Lakes. Now, if the manufacturers of Canada have five million people to supply instead of two millions or less as at present, look at what advantage it will be to them. I want to say to the manuiacturers that it will behoove them to just be a little careful because as hon. gentlemen opposite know the people of the three prairie provinces are to a large extent low tariff people whether they are Liberals or Conservatives,-of which we have evidence by certain motions moved by these gentlemen on the other side,-and if the manufacturers insist on looking for trouble they will be very apt to find it in the end. Therefore, in heir own interest the manufacturers ought to be careful. "Why, the grain growers, the farmers and the people of the west generally are the most reasonable people on the face of the earth. They want a square deal; thev do r.ot want to be hewers of wood and drawers of water inr all time to come. The day has gone when you could make a farmer in the west or in the east either believe that protection protects him, but at the same time they are willing to pay their fair share towards meeting the expenses of the country. There are a good many things on which the tariff must be reduced, but if we get this agreement through and secure the American market for the products of the Canadian farmer, we will have made a great step in the right direction, and the people of the west will be reasonably well satisfied. Let me tell you that if this agreement is not carried into effect there will be a general agitation that will never be put down until there is a reduction of the tariff all around, which would take in a great deal more manufactured articles than this agreement deals with. I speak for the western farmers principally-there are gentlemen in this House who can speak for the eastern farmers-I speak for the western farmers in what I say as to this agreement. It has been stated time and again in this House, by Igentlemen opposite that the American market is not. as good as the Canadian market and will therefore be of no advantage to us. Even supposing that were true we do not stand to lose anything. If the American market is lower than the
Canadian market we won't ship our goods there, and we do not lose the British market, nor do we lose our home market. But as a matter of fact that is not so. I lived for twenty years on the prairie right near the American boundary, and I make the statement that from the day the territory of Saskatchewan had a bushel of wheat for sale-I do not speak as to the last two years, because I have no personal knowledge as to that period-but previous to the last two years there never was a year during which at some time of the season the Canadian farmer could not draw his wheat across the line and get for it from five cents to ten cents a bushel more than he could get at home.

speechtext: And pay the duty?

speechtext: No, and under this agreement he won't have any duty to pay.

I am not going to say that wheat should have been ten cents higher on the American side, but I do say that there has never been a year when the big milling associations and the big wheat exporters and domestic buyers have not been able to put the price down below the actual value of the wheat in Canada, and so, by taking it across the line our farmers got better prices. I know what I am talking about, because I have grown wheat in the west and I have bought wheat and I have sold wheat. I do not say that at all times of the year there is that difference or that there will be that difference in the future at all times of the year, but I say there has been a better market generally all along the border line on the American side than on the Canadian side, and we will get the advantage of that when this agreement is put in force. But wheat is not the only article the western farmers have to sell. They grow a great deal of flax and a great deal of barley in my section of the country, and I will give you an actual incident that has taken place.
About a month ago one of my constituents spent a few days with me in Ottawa. He is a farmer in the western portion of my district, an educated and wealthy man, a young man who went out there twelve or fifteen years ago as a school teacher, who has now made enough money to retire easily if he wished to, although he is still a young man. He told me that last year he had as a side crop 2,000 bushels of flax. Last year it cost him exactly $500 in cold cash to put that flax into Duluth, where practically all the flax from that part of the country goes. There is a duty of 25 cents a bushel on flax entering the United States, and that made $500 on his 2,000 bushels, which went

into the coffers of the United States treasury. If he could have loaded his car on the American instead of the Canadian side of the line he would have got exactly $500 more for his two carloads of flax than he did get. As he said to me in my house:	Do
you think you are going to make me more loyal to Great Britain or more loyal to Canada by taking $500 out of my pocket on one side crop in one year? He said, the thing is absurd; if I had that $500 I would not bury it in the earth, that money would have been in circulation and a great deal of it would have got back again to the east in payment for manufactured goods. That is only one farmer; I have scores and scores of farmers who raise from 500 to 2,000 bushels of flax. In the southern portion of the district of Regina there are hundreds of thousands of bushels of flax raised and there will be a great deal more in the future, because if you get a market for your flax without paying 25 cents duty, our farmers will grow a great deal more, and the day will come when we will have to grow less wheat. This very season if we should happen to strike a good crop in the west we will have in the three prairie provinces more wheat for export than Great Britain ever bought in any one year.

speechtext:
I am trying to tell my hon. friend that there would be no duty to pay, and that the farmer would get a better price for his products. Now, my hon. friend is a doubting Thomas, and I am going to convince him, if he can be convinced. I was in Winnipeg less than a month ago, and one rancher from Alberta, not far from the boundary line, made the statement that last fall he had sold between 200 and 300 steers to be
delivered at the railway-and let me say here that when cattle are sold in the west, it does not matter to whom they are sold, those for export go to Gordon and Ironsides, and those to be butchered go to Pat Bums. Before this man could get his cattle rounded up, twelve of the steers had drifted across to the American side of the line. The boundary line there is not visible, at least, the cattle do not know when they cross it. On each side of the line there is a Cattlemen's Association, and the association in Montana look after all stray cattle, and, as a rule, every stray animal that is fit for market is shipped to the market at once, in order to get it off the grass, which is wanted for the cattle that are not fit for the market. These twelve stray animals were shipped to Chicago, the freight was paid on them, the commission was paid to the man who sold them and exchange was paid on the money coming back, and this rancher on the Canadian side said that a few months afterwards he got a cheque for the twelve steers, and it amounted to exactly $8 a head more than he had got for the cattle that he sold at home. In the face of these facts, what man is going to say that reciprocity is not good for the western farmer?

speechtext: I want to say a word or two about some of the bankers. I refer more particularly to the letter written by Sir Edmund Walker. Some ancient said, ' Oh, that mine enemy would write me a letter.' Well, if the Liberal party had sat up every night for a month, I think they could not have made any better literature for themselves than the letter Sir Edmund Walker wrote.

speechtext: What about the farmers?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I am speaking as a representative of the farmers. If Sir Edmund Walkejr had given the matted a second thought, he would not have been so ready to fly to the newspapers on the question of reciprocity. If there is any

class of people who have been well treated by all governments in Canada it is the bankers. Just let us see what position they occupy; and I am not going to criticise what has been done for them. I believe it has been in the interests of the country generally to give them what they have been given, but there are some things they have been doing that I think are open to criticism. I am going to give some figures which I have taken from the returns in the Canada ' Gazette ' of April 20. I find, after deducting the 5 per cent of the circulation which the bankers have to put up to guarantee the notes of all the banks, that the banks of Canada have at the present moment $77,364,134 of bank bills for which they do not pay one cent of interest, they have also deposits of $278,171,792, that do not bear interest, making a total of $355,535,925 which they get from the people of Canada absolutely free of cost; and they get that money to loan it out to .you and me or any one else who has to borrow it, at 6 per cent, and when times get a little hard, they charge us 7 per cent. In addition, they have $533,032,466 for which they pay at the outside 3 per cent. Then they have at the present time invested in the United States $149,477,172. As I have said, I quite believe in the policy of putting the banks in a good- position. I think it has been all right to give them that currency free. I think it all right for the banks to take that $149,000,000 down to Uncle Sam's territory and use it to move the southern cotton crop and to loan it out on call loans at from two to fifty per cent according to the state of the market; because I realize that if they did not do that, they would have the money more or less idle at home. But what I do object to is that while Sir Edmund Walker took the millions from his bank and sent them to New York and Chicago to make money for his shareholders without affecting their loyalty or the Royalty of himself, he thinks that the farmer, who puts up that money, cannot be allowed to sell a steer, or a horse or a pig, or a carload of barley, or flax in the United States without becoming a disloyal man, ready to disrupt the empire. Did you ever hear anything more absurd in your life?

speechtext:
You are not going to ^stampede me or rattle me. I got up to say a few things, and I am going to say them. The fact that you like them or the fact that you do not like them will not make any difference.
Now, I wish to take up the question of railways for a minute. The hon. member Mr. TURRIFF.
for Terrebonne (Mr. Nantel), was very much afraid that the railway traffic was going to be diverted to the south. He said that J. J. Hill had a number of lines built on the American side close to the Canadian boundary, and if this amendment went into force, all our traffic would go into the United States. Well, let us look at the situation for a moment. The Canadian Pacific railway, the only transcontinental line in Canada that is completed, has one road from the west to the east. But how many lines has it west of Winnipeg running from Canada into the United States? One would think, to hear hon. members on the other side talk about the disloyalty of trading with the United States, and the danger of ruining the Canadian Pacific railway, that the Canadian Pacific railway would be very anxious to keep away from the United States. But the Canadian Pacific railway has some seven lines, built by themselves without any assistance from Canada, and without any request from the people of Canada to build them, running from Canadian territory into the United States-six or seven lines west of Winnipeg. And the Great Northern railway and the Canadian Northern railway have each two or three lines running into the United States in the same way. Was it disloyal to build these lines running into the United States? And as to our traffic being diverted to the United States, I just want to say this: The Canadian Pacific railway was largely built by the people of Canada. The Grand Trunk railway is being largely built by the people of Canada. The Canadian Northern railway is being largely built by the people of Canada. The Canadian Pacific railway is the only completed road, and it has the shortest line from the prairies of the west to tidewater. It has a line 275 miles shorter than any American road. And if, with the shortest road and with -a railway more than half built for them, they cannot carry this traffic as cheaply as the American lines which would have to pay for every dollar of their construction, then the Canadian Pacific railway ought to lose the traffic. If they want to retain the traffic all they have to do is ts^ lower their freight rates. And look at the position:	The Canadian Pacific railway is paying not only interest on its bonds and dividends on its preferred stock, but it is also paying 10 per cent on its common stock which is largely composed of water. The Canadian Pacific railway during the last half year set apart as a rest no less than $10,500,000, and in the previous half another $10,000,000; that is, in one year they set aside $20,500,000 as a rest fund. And last year they paid 9 per cent, and they are to pay 10 per cent in the future. So, I say, all they have to do in order to retain the trade of the country is to lower

freight rates, and I can assure you their freight rates would stand lowering. I heard of one extraordinary instance, and I want to take advantage of the opportunity new to bring it to the attention of the Minister of Railways. It seems to me it raises the question as to whether the Railway Commission of Canada should not be instructed to look into its tariffs and find out if they are not iniquitous, and not wait for the individual who has suffered injustice to bring a case before them. If a merchant or manufacturer in Ottawa wishes to send a carload of goods, half, let us say of class 5 and the other half class 6, he can ship that to any place from here to Halifax or from here to Port Arthur, paying the carload rate on the higher class. But, if he ships to west of Port Arthur, he cannot get a carload rate at all; he has to pay by the 100 pounds. If that is true-and I believe it is -it is iniquitous, and it is a matter for the Railway Commission to take up, not waiting for anybody who suffers the injustice to bring their attention to it.
Now, when I started to speak I promised some of my friends that I would not occupy more than three-quarters of an hour. I have taken up about that time, and I do not wish to take up any more. I am thoroughly in sympathy with the agreement; I believe it is the best bargain the government of Canada has ever made and that it is a 'bargain that will lead to increased prosperity for the country. I have been seven years in this House and before that I was often in the gallery a listener. And, so far as I know-and if I am wrong my right hon. friend the leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) can correct me-there has never been a year I think, when hon. members opposite did not come forward with resolutions denouncing the policy of the government, and trying to show that the country was not as prosperous as it ought to be. But, since this reciprocity agreement was introduced, hon. members opposite have changed their tune altogether, and, they declare, like the hon. member for Terrebonne, the country is now so prosperous it would be a crime to make any change. If hon. members opposite are right now, they have been wrong for fourteen years. According to the theory of probabilities they were more likely to be honest when they went thirteen times in successive years in one direction than now when, to suit their political exigencies, they try to make out that this is not a good agreement. If there were no politics in this, not one in twenty of them would be against this agreement. So, I hope the right hon. Prime Minister will go right on with this question, pound it right through and not take back water for a moment. It is the will of the people, and we were sent here to represent the people. We believe that 258
this agreement is a right thing; and for my part 1 am satisfied that if this agreement is put in force, a new era of prosperity will dawn for Canada, even greater prosperity than we have had in the past; and I believe that Canada will grow and thrive and occupy an even higher position in the great sisterhood of nations making up the British Empire to which we are so proud to belong.
