speechtext:
My constituency in the province of Manitoba is situated a good deal the same as that of the hon. member (Mr. Turriff), who has just taken his seat. My constituency extends along the international boundary for about eighty miles. The farmers in my constituency can see the farmers across the line receiving a higher price for their wheat, they can see the farmers across the line receiving a higher price for their barley, and as my hon. friend says, they also get a higher price for their stockers. I saw the apparent relief that this Bill would give our people, on the 26th day of January when the Finance Minister unfolded this plan to the House. I saw that it would apparently be an advantage to them, I .saw that our people might possibly get a better price for those articles. But let me ask, is this the relief that the people of western Canada have been asking for? Is this the relief that they are entitled to? I say no, not by any means. On account of this apparent relief to the people in my constituency, I received many resolutions from the grain growers asking me to support this proposition of reciprocity, but after listening to the discussion in this House and studying the question for myself, I decided that so far as I was concerned I would not support it. Apparently the people in my constituency wanted it; the men who had voted for me and sent me here apparently wanted it. If they wanted it, and I had decided not to vote for it, what was my duty under the circumstances? I made up my mind to go home and to lay the matter plainly before my constituents, and if a majority of my supporters still wanted it, then I was prepared to resign my seat and allow them to send some one else who would vote for it. In order to ascertain their opinion I held four meetings within the local constituencies in the Dominion constituency of Lisgar and gave every person an opportunity to attend the meetings. After I had held those meetings and explained my position fully, I asked all those men who had voted for me in the election of 1908, to remain, as I wished to go into the matter a little more fully with them, and I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that after I had laid my ideas before them, there was only one man at all



those meetings who stood up and voted for reciprocity, and opposed my stand. Notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), has said, I am satisfied that when the people of Canada understand this deal they will reject it entirely. This government has forced through the Autonomy Bill without submitting it to the people, they have forced through the Grand Trunk Pacific deal without submitting it to the people, last year they forced through the Navy Bill without submitting it to the people, but I want to tell the Prime Minister that the Conservative party in this House will not allow this deal to go through until it has been submitted to the people. We are prepared at any time to abide by the will of the people, and we now ask the Prime Minister to submit this question to the people, and I am satisfied that when he does so we will come back from western Canada stronger than we are now.
The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has gone into the conditions in western Canada. Who is responsible for those conditions? Why, it is the Prime Minister of this country, who has held the reigns of power during the past fifteen years and has not done one thing yet for the grain growers or farmers of Canada, He has allowed them to be fleeced in every way. Sir, what are the conditions in western Canada at the present time? The beef combine and the pork combine have driven the producers out of business entirely, and that is the chief reason for the high price of those articles in western Canada at the present time. Time and again we have appealed to this government for relief, and they have refused it. Take this cement combine. The government allowed that cement combine to be formed, and helped it through. Our people in western Canada are using more cement every year. In my little town of Manitou we put down cement sidewalks to the value of $13,000 or $14,000 before this cement combine was organized. If we had waited until after the combine had been formed to buy our cement, it would have cost us $1,300 or $1,400 more. My hon. friend from Assiniboia has said that the railway companies are robbing the people of western Canada, and that is true, as every one knows who is acquainted with the conditions. Our people are paying twenty to eighty per cent higher rates than the people are paying on the^ other side of the line, and the Prime Minister of this country is responsible for it. The wheat combine are manipulating grades and prices and are trimming the farmers, there is no doubt about that. The farmers on the other side of the line get higher prices than we do. Again, the Prime Minister is responsible for that. The implement com-

speechtext:
panies are charging us a third more than they should for our implements, at least we think so. Take a case that occurred at Miami, in the province of Manitoba. Three farmers there who were growing corn wanted to buy a corn binder, and they went to the three different companies who were selling binders in the town of Miami. The Deering Company and the McCormick Company offered to sell a binder for $150.
I understand that corn binders are not manufactured in Canada by those companies and these companies import them and pay duty on them. Then these farmers went to the Massey-Harris Company who asked $160 for a binder, the same article, without paying any duty at all. That is the condition of affairs in western Canada at the present time. Is it, therefore, any wonder that the people are ready to grab at anything which looks like relief to them? There is a combine to keep up the prices of every thing they have to buy, and there is a combine to keep down the prices of everything they have to sell. That is the condition the government has allowed to grow up during the past fifteen years. That is the condition the Prime Minister found when he went to western Canada last summer. At every point he was met by a delegation of farmers who asked for relief. But the Prime Minister knew that he and his government were not strong enough to cope with those conditions they had allowed to grow up.
What did he do? Why, Mr. Chairman he gave us reciprocity with the United States as a cure-all for the troubles m western Canada. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) made the statement that he had it on the authority of the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance that they had gone as far as they intended to go_ in the interests of the producers of this country. Afterwards, when it was put up to the Prime Minister he said, yes, the hon. member for North Oxford had that authority. I want to tell the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance that the grain growers of western Canada, the only time they ever had an opportunity of pronouncing upon this proposal, absolutely refused to endorse it. At the time the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Finance were in western Canada, in 1905, they put this proposition up to the grain growers and they refused it unless the duties on everything were lowered to a revenue basis of 17 per cent. I just wish to read the resolution that was submitted to these hon. gentlemen at that time. This was moved by Mr. Andrew Graham, one of our grain growers in western Canada:
Resolved, that in the opinion of the executive of the Manitoba Grain Growers' Association and the Manitoba Live Stock Association,

816G
the present tariff on dutiable goods be reduced to a revenue tariff of an average of 17 per cent; that all goods at present on the free list be retained thereon with the addition thereto of all kinds of lumber; that in consideration of this reduction to a revenue tariff we are willing to have all agricultural products placed on the free list.
That was the only proposition that the grain growers of western Canada ever presented to the government of this country, and that is a proposition to which the government refused to accede. It is true that the grain growers, when they were here on the 16th December last, presented a resolution to the government in connection with reciprocity, but there was not one word in any way, shape, or form, in connection with reciprocity in the original resolutions passed by the grain growers associations throughout the western country. Reciprocity was never spoken of in connection with these resolutions until the delegation arrived in the city of Ottawa. I am credibly informed that it is an absolute fact that on the arrival of the grain growers from western Canada a certain gentleman visited the Prime Minister and there was hatched the resolution in connection with reciprocity.
I wish to say a word or two with reference to a publication we have in the city of Winnipeg known as the ' Grain Growers' Guide.' Last fall the ' Grain Growers' Guide ' came out with an editorial saying that they were going to send a representative to the press gallery in this House, and that this reporter would give an unbiassed report of everything that took place in regard to western Canada during his term here. But, on the 15th of March this paper came out with a very severe attack on the Conservative members from western Canada. They called us blockers, objectors, obstructors, and they almost called us traitors to the people we represent. They also claimed that we had voted against reciprocity. I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that if there is one principle that this paper has stood for during the time in which it has been in existence, from the very first issue that came out, it is the referendum and recall. That is one of the cardinal principles of this ' Grain Growers' Guide,' and I thought for one that if we ever had an opportunity of voting for submitting any question to the people of this country we would get credit for it from this paper, instead of what we did receive. I wish to read the resolution that this paper condemned us so violently for voting for. It was moved by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, and it reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this House the said resolutions should not be proceeded with until the electors have had an opportunity of pronouncing upon their merits.
We simply wanted to have this recipro city deal submitted to the people of this country. That is what I voted for, and that is what we all voted for. But, that did not suit the ' Grain Growers' Guide ' and they went for us in the manner I speak of. When it came to the question of the terminal elevators, a question that is of vital importance to the grain growers, my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Sehaffner) moved a resolution, every Conservative in this House voted for that resolution, and every reformer voted against it, but the ' Grain Growers' Guide ' never mentioned all the names in connection with that proposition whatever. The same thing took place in connection with the chilled meat trade. My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) brought in a resolution in connection with the establishment of a chilled meat trade in this country. Every Conservative voted for it and every Reformer against it, but the ' Grain Growers' Guide ' never mentioned all the names in connection with the matter, and how each man voted. They only mentioned the names of those speaking on the different questions. I consider that the ' Grain Growers' Guide ' has forfeited the confidence of the grain growers of western Canada. My hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) has said that reciprocity is the most important question that has come before the people of Canada since confederation, but in my humble judgment it is the most important question that has ever come before our people, even including confederation, because as we all know confederation was adopted to unite the different provinces together, and the direct outcome of confederation was the building of the Canadian Pacific railway, which has been followed, through the sacrifices made by the people of Canada during the past forty-two years, by three transcontinental railways which are now almost completed. But, is this reciprocity pact calculated to bind the Canadian communities closer together, is it meant to further build up the interprovincial trade we have established? I say it is not. If it should be carried into effect, Alberta and British Columbia will deal with the western states, Saskatchewan and Manitoba will deal with the Dakotas and Minnesota, Ontario and the eastern provinces will deal with the eastern states, and instead of having our lines running from east to west as now, the outcome will be that our lines will be running north and south. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Turriff) also said that both parties in this country have been trying for many years to get reciprocity with the United States. I wish to say that in my humble judgment, what was good for this country between 1854 and 1866 might be a very bad thing for the country in 1911. Canada is a very difficult country to govern; our seven and a half

millions of people are located in a narrow territory, 100 miles wide and 3,500 miles long, and the diversified conditions of commercial interest, and racial distinctions, make it one of the most difficult countries in the known world to govern. But, if we want to build this country up to what we all hope to see it some day, we must in each province be prepared to give and take. We hear from the different provinces a great deal about class legislation. Just look for a moment at what we have been fighting for for western Canada since I have been in this parliament, and what the grain growers asked for on the 16th of December last. They asked for government ownership and operation of the terminal elevators, for government ownership and operation of the Hudson Bay railway, for the establishement of a chilled meat trade throughout western Canada, and these three things alone would cost $75,000,000 or thereabouts. And, while eastern Canada will have to help build up western Canada in these things, there are other things in respect to which the west will help to build up eastern Canada, and there are other things which will be of special advantage to British Columbia, and in which the prairie provinces can assist. We must, therefore, be prepared to give and take in the building up of a great diversified country such as we have in Canada. The Prime Minister has changed his mind a good deal on this reciprocity question since 1899, because in that year he spoke as follows, as reported in ' Hansard ':
If we know the hearts and minds of our people at present, I think I am not making too wide a statement when I say that the general feeling in Canada is not in favour of reciprocity. There was a time when Canada would have given many things to obtain the American market; there rwas a time when the market of the great cities of the union was the only market iwe had, but these things are past and over now. We are not depending on the American markets now.
That was the idea of the Prime Minister in 1899. The United States left us alone for forty-five years, and absolutely refused to have anything to do with us in trade relations, and why is it they ask at this particular juncture for a reciprocity deal with the people of Canada? The best answer to that question is to be found in the words of President Taft's message to Congress on the 26th of January, 1911, when he said:
The Dominion has greatly prospered. It has an active, aggressive, intelligent people. They are coming to the parting of the ways. In the reciprocal trade agreement numerous additions are made to the free list. These include not only food commodities such as cattle, fish, wheat and other grain, fresh vegetables, fruit and dairy products, but also rough lumber and raw material useful to our own industries. Free lumber we ought to have. By giving our people access to the Mr. SHAKPE (Lisgar).
Canadian forests we should reduce the consumption of our own, which in the hands of a comparatively few owners now have a value that requires the enlargement of our available timber resources.
I think these words of President Taft answer the question a good deal better than I can. I would like to give a short list of the natural resources of Canada that the United States would like to get hold of; it is estimated that we have 500,000,000,000 feet of standing timber; our wheat fields are about 600 miles wide by 1,000 miles long in western Canada; it is estimated that we have 117,000,000 acres of wheat lands, 12,500 miles of coast fishing; 440,000 square miles of fresh water fishing, our coal is estimated at 172,000,000,000 tons, we have produced $260,000,000 worth of gold, our silver mines are the third most important in the world: we have three-fifths of the world's supply of nickel, in 1901 we produced 160,000,000 tons of iron and in 1904 we produced 509,000,000 tons of iron.
We have untold millions of tons of iron. Our water-powers are estimated at 25,000,-0C0, and of fisheries $30,000,000. This is only a partial list for we have in this northern country the greatest undeveloped country in minerals $90,000,000; of timber cut $63,000,000, and of fisheries $30,000,000. This is only a partial list for we have in this northern county the greatest undeveloped country in the known world. It is these natural resources that the United States are after, and these, if this Bill goes through, we will allow them to exploit. Why do they want our natural resources? Theirs are almost gone, they have wasted their natural resources in the past, and now they want the natural resources in this northern country to keep the flame of prosperity going in the United States. Are we prepared to hand over to the United States the prosperity that is coming to Canada? We stand to-day just about where the United States stood 100 years ago, and for my part I say:	Keep the natural
resources for the Canadian people. They want our hard wheat to mix with their soft wheat to sell in the markets of the world to compete against our wheat. They want our bran and shorts to feed to their cattle and hogs, to compete against our cattle and pork in the markets of the world, But if we want to import any of that same bran and shorts, ground from our own wheat back into our own country to feed our own stock, we must pay a duty on it of 12J cents.
But some say the United States can do this anyway, by simply taking off the duty. I say if the United States want to do that, let them do it. Why should we pull the rope that will hang ourselves? I am not prepared to do it. But even if they did do that, it would not let in 12 other foreign

countries into our markets, nor would it admit all the British possessions throughout the world into the Canadian market while we have only the one market opened to us. These markets will all be closed to the people of Canada and there will be only the one market for us. The countries which will have the same privileges in our market as the United States under this Bill are the following: Austria-Hungary, Argentine Republic, Bolivia, Colombia, Denmark, Japan, Norway, Russia Spain, Sweden, Venezuela and France, besides all the British possessions. In addition to opening our market to these countries, I would point out that we pay in subsidies to steamship companies, plying between Canada and these countries, over $1,000,000 a year, and thus these ships will be able to bring the products of these countries that much cheaper to our markets to compete against our people.
Some say that there is no danger of any of these countries sending anything into Canada. Let us look for a moment at the products shipped by these countries into Canada during 1910, in the face of a fairly high duty:

The United States people do not need our wheat for consumption in the United States, because they are exporters of wheat and flour, as we are and will be for the next 50 or 100 years, as I shall show. They are producing more wheat every year. These figures are taken from ' Reciprocity with Canada,' being the White-book of the United States, on page 94. In 1908 the United States produced 634,000,000 bushels of wheat, in 1909, 664,000,000 bushels, an increase of 30,000,000 bushels; in 1910 they produced 737,000,000, or 72,000,000 bushels more than in 1909; so that they are going on producing more and more wheat every year. This proves that they Mr. SHARPE (Lisgar).
do not need the wheat of our country for consumption. When the Reform orators go through the country saying that they are opening up the markets of 90,000,000 people for Canada, it sounds pretty good to the people throughout the country; there is no doubt about that. But I would like to ask you, Mr. Chairman, what good are the markets of those 90,000,000 people if they are producing the same goods as we are, year after year, only in far larger quantities. If the markets of those 90,000,000 people are good for the farmers throughout Canada, surely the same markets would be good for the biscuits manufactured by the Minister of Customs or for the coa'l produced in the province from which the Minister of Finance comes. But we find that they do not want the markets of those 90,000,000 people for their own manufactures or the products of their own province. These 90,000,000 people are exporting the same goods that we are, year after year, onlv in far larger quantities. I wish to state a few of the items that they are exporting at the present time. In 1908 they exported 151,000,000 bushels of wheat, 37,000,000 bushe'ls of corn, 14,000,000 bushels of oatmeal, 2,333,000 bushels of oats, 8,262,000 bushels of barley, $9,303,000 worth of flaxseed or linseed oil cake, and 437,000 bushels of flaxseed. It is true they are not exporting as much raw material as they did in the past; but when you look up the manufactured articles that they are exporting, you will see that they are exporting more and more of them every year. In 1905 they exported $42,000,000 worth of meal and flour, and in 1908 $66,000,000 worth, an increase of $24,000,000. Look at their exports of live animals and meats. Of live animals they exported in 1906 $49,000,000 worth, and in 1909 $ 22,000,000 worth, showing that they are not shipping as many live animals. But look at the finished article. Of beef, fresh and cured, they exported in 1905 $47,000,000 worth, and in 1908 $51,000,000 worth. Of pork, cured and fresh, they exported in 1905, $106,000,000 worth, and in 1908	$121,-
000,000 worth, an increase of $15,000,000. The	total animal matter exported in 1905 was $224,000,000 worth, and in 1908 $238,000,000 worth. In the face of these figures, I would like to ask what good the markets of the United States w:ll be to us in Canada. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat told us how much better price we would get for our export cattle. I believe that he is very largely correct. For stockers also we would get perhaps a little better price. But take dairy cows, and you will find that they are higher in Manitoba than in North Dakota. The price in North Dakota is from

$33 to $39 per head, whi'le in western Canada the price is from $39 to $41 per head. I would like to ask, is it the proper policy for the people of western Canada, or any other part of Canada, to sell their Stockers to the United States? I say it is not. If the government would establish what the grain-growers have asked for, and what the Conservative party in this House has voted for, that is, a chilled meat trade throughout western Canada, they would drive out of business the beef combines of western Canada, and secure for the producers there a decent price for the products of their cattle. This deal will let in the beef trust of the United States. I wish to read what the grain-growers had to say on this question, on the 16th of December last, when they were here. They did not ask for reciprocity for their cattle by any means. They asked for the very opposite of that. They prayed the government to keep out the beef trust of the United States, but by this very deal the government are going to al'low the beef trust of the United States to come and get control of the markets of Canada. This is what the delegation of the western farmers asked for, as will be found on page 27 of the report:
We wish also to draw attention to the danger we are in while we leave the opportunity open for the United States meat interest to capture and control the export trade from our country. We contend that it is a very vital importance, if the Canadian meat trade is to grow and prosper as our natural resources will permit, that Canada must have her own route and equipment. Another serious condition arises when from any cause a crop is of poor quality, and there is not sufficient stock in the country to consume it. Still another complication, due to the poor and uncertain price for beef, is the deterioration of our beef animals through crossing of dairy breeds with them and the tendency to careless breeding of inferior stock.
The farmers, in view of this situation, believe that the remedy for this condition of affairs is the establishment of an export trade in dressed beef.
That is what the western farmers asked for in December last, and you are doing the very opposite. The beef trust of the United States went into the British market a short time ago, and opened stalls throughout England, and they found one of their strongest competitors in a firm called Park Brothers, who could compete with them, and who did compete with them in the selling of meat to consumers in England. The beef trust wanted to get rid of Park Brothers, and what did they do? They started to hunt up where the supply was coming from that Park Brothers were receiving. They went to the Argentine Republic and looked into the conditions there. They found that Park Brothers were getting
their cattle from three large ranches in that country, and that they had a contract with these ranches to supply them with meat for five years. But there was a proviso in the contract that if, at any time the ranches were sold, the contract was to be terminated. And what happened? The Beef Trust of the United States bought up these three ranches in the Argentine Republic and put Park Brothers out of business. The meat trust of the United States went to Australia and was going to try and get control there. But the government of Australia met them at the wharf with both hands raised in warning and said:	We
dont want you; stay away from our country; we want our people to get a fair deal. But this government is satisfied to open our markets freely to the beef trust of the United States. What we need for the beef trade of this country and especially in western Canada is the establishment of chilled meat trade operated and owned by the government, so that our people may be assured of getting a fair deal. They have not been getting a fair deal in the past, but have been robbed time and time again. And, as I have said, this government has been appealed to many times by the beef producers and pork producers of western Canada, but it has always turned a deaf ear to their plea.
Sheep also are higher in price in Canada than in the United (States. The price throughout Canada varies from $4 to $7 per head, but in the United States it varies from $3.90 to $5.30. Swine also are higher in Canada than in the United States; the average price throughout Canada is from $10 to $13, while the average price throughout the United States is $10 to $11. The fruit question would be affected by this agreement in a way that would be beneficial to my constituency-no doubt about that. Any person who buys fruit knows that free fruit will be an advantage to western Canada. But, while that is true, it is also true that the fruit growers of British Columbia and the fruit growers of eastern Canada will have to pay their share towards the terminal elevators, and towards the Hudson Bay railway, and towards the establishment of the chilled meat trade. And that being so, surely, the people of western Canada are manly and loyal _ enough to pay a fair price for their fruit. I was here . on the floor of this House when the fifteen hundred fruit growers came into this Chamber and laid their case before the government. I heard them tell about how their work was being ruined by this deal, and I heard them state that they represented capital to the amount of $200,000,000. These men had spent their lives in building up homes and fruit orchards, and they saw that they were t >
be entirely ruined in

one night by this deal. I heard their explanation that the early fruit from the United States would be shipped into Canada, and in that way would kill the market in Canada. For we all know that when a man goes down street in the early fruit season, if he sees a bunch of grapes or other fruit in the window it looks very tempting and there is no doubt that he will pay two or three prices for it. These fruit men claimed that it. was from the early crop they made their money, and that the later crop would only pay expenses. And what did the Prime Minister answer these fifteen hundred Canadians who had come to present their requests to him? Was it what it should have been?-Here you are, fifteen hundred Canadians, and I am the Prime Minister of Canada:	I will investigate
your case, and if what you say is right I will remedy the trouble. That is not the answer they received. On the contrary the answer they received was:	Your doom is
sealed; the pact is signed, sealed and delivered to the United States people; you are too late; there is no use in your coming to me, if you want relief you must go to Washington, not to Ottawa. I say I know that the people of western Canada are manly enough to pay a decent price for their fruit and to help these men against competition from the United States.
Then, there is the oats question. Of course, there has not been much discussion of this on the other side of the House, because of course oats are higher in Canada than in the United States. The United States in 1910 produced 1,126,765,000 bushels of oats, and the average price to the farmer in the United States was 34 cents a bushel. We produced in Canada 325,500,000 bushels, and the average price to the farmer in Canada was 35 cents a bushel. They produced in South Dakota in the same year 35,075,000 bushels at an average price of 30 cents a bushel. We produced in Manitoba 41,000,000 bushels of oats, and the average price paid the farmer throughout Manitoba was 31 cents a bushel. So, I do not think there is any use wasting more time on that subject.
There has been a good deal of discussion in connection with the barley trade; the question has been taken up by almost every speaker on that side who has spoken on this measure. It would hardly do for me to pass it by without saying a few words. In 1910 the United States produced 162,237,000 bushels of barley.
The average price paid to the farmer throughout the United States for that year was 57 cents per bushel. The United States exported 8,262,961 bushels of barley. We produced in Canada 45,147,000 bushels, and the average price paid to the Canadian farmer was 47 cents per bushel. We export-Mr. SHARPE (Lisgar).
ed 1,446,307 bushels. South Dakota produced 20,727,000 bushels, and the average price paid to the farmer was 51 cents. Western members will recollect that last year North Dakota produced very little barley, and they had none to sell, consequently I am using the figures for South Dakota. Manitoba produced 13,836,000 bushels of barley, and the average- price paid to the farmer was 39 cents per' bushel, or a difference of 12 cents between the price the Manitoba farmer received and the price the South Dakota farmer received. Now, it looks at first sight as if our farmers in western Canada would receive this extra 12 cents per bushel if the duty was taken off. But I wish to direct your attention to this fact, that while the South Dakota farmer received 51 cents a bushel for his barley, the Minnesota farmer, a state lying alongside South Dakota, received 60 cents a bushel for his barley, a difference of 9 cents in two states under the same tariff. In Montana the farmer received 62 cents a bushel, in Wisconsin 64 cents, in Maine 76 cents, or a difference of 26 cents a bushel between the price in South Dakota and the price in Maine. Up to 1894 the duty on barley going into the United States was 30 cents a bushel. In that year it was changed to 30 per cent ad valorem which meant a reduction to about 15 cents a bushel. Now the very year the duty was lowered on barley going into the United States, the price throughout the whole of the United States dropped 11 cents a bushel. Some may claim that this was because of a large crop that year, and I thought perhaps that might be the case. Therefore, I took the three years before the duty was lowered, the three years during which the duty was lowered, and then the three years after the duty was put back to its former point, Let me read again from the White Book called 'Reciprocity with Canada/ at page 101, where I find that in the years 1892, 1893 and 1894 the average price of barley throughout the United States was 44 cents per bushel; during the next three years, 1895, 1896 and 1897, during which the duty was lowered to practically 15 cents a bushel, the average price was 34 cents a bushel. Then at the end of these three years when the duty was put back to 30 cents a bushel, that is for 1898, 1899, 1900, the price throughout the United States went up to 43 cents a bushel. Now I would ask any fair-minded man what would the price of barley be in Canada the moment the duty was taken off entirely? It is my opinion that we would not receive one cent more for our barley in western Canada than we do at the present time if the duty was taken off. According to the official report of the Board of the Agricultural college, it takes three to three and a half lbs. of barley to produce one pound of pork. The ' Farmers' Sun ' gives the average price of Canadian pork for the
81T7

last ten years as $7 per 100 lbs. Taking three and a half lbs. of barley to one lb. of pork would give 96 cents per bushel; taking three lbs. of barley to one lb. of pork would give $1.12 per bushel. So according to these undisputed authorities it works out that the Canadian farmer, by feeding his barley, realizes from 96 cents to $1.12 per bushel, in addition to which he has the by-products to enrich his farm.
Now I wish to deal shortly with the wheat question. Most of our friends think there is not going to be much gain to our farmers on the wheat question if this deal should go through. I will quote from the 'Agricultural Year Book' of the United States, and by the way this is where I get the most of the figures that I have given to-night, except when I have quoted from the 'White Book on Reciprocity with Canada and the United States.' And I find by these records that the United States exported in 1906,
127,000,000 bushels of wheat, and in 1908 it exported 151,000,000 bushels. The average price paid to the farmers throughout Canada was 93 cents a bushel ; the average price paid to the farmer of North Dakota is 90 cents a bushel ; the average price paid to the farmer in Manitoba was 80 cents a bushel. Now these figures look as if there would be some advantage to the farmers of Manitoba if they could get this extra 10 cents a bushel. But I wish to remind you that the millers of Minneapolis are no doubt paying the farmers of North Dakota a premium on their hard wheat at the present time. The moment the markets of the United States are opened to the people of western Canada and our 63,000,000 bushels of surplus wheat are thrown upon their markets this price will go down to an absolute export basis. They will no longer pay a premium on hard wheat at the Minneapolis mills. Take the condition at Morden and Plum Coulee at the present time; the Great Northern have branches in there from the United States and they can ship our wheat through in bond, grind it, ship it out again and it will only involve a duty of about one-quarter of one per cent. Do they pay our people as high a price as they pay in the United States? Not by any means. Our buyers in Manitoba are beating them out at every point. At Plum Coulee our buyers ship by the Canadian route about 100,000 bushels while they only ship 20,000 bushels through the United States. If they wanted our wheat and would pay a price of from 8 to 10 a bushel more they could take all the wheat from every point they touch, but they do not do it. I would like the Minister of Agriculture to explain to us-he took very good care not to touch upon it at the time he made his speech-why it is that the farmers in Quebec received $1.19
a bushel for their wheat while the Ontario farmer only receives 89 cents a bushel. If the Minister of Agriculture will explain that I will give way.

speechtext: I might be tempted to suggest that we have better wheat in Quebec, but I do not suppose my hon. friend will accept that explanation.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
subtopic: IMPORTS INTO CANADA FOR HOME CONSUMPTION FROM MOST FAVOURED NATION COUNTRIES DURING SIX YEARS.
speechtext:
I do not know.
I would like to have it explained any way because it is something that has puzzled me ever since I have seen the figures. The South Dakota farmer received 89 cents a bushel for his wheat while the farmer in Minnesota, the very next state, received 94 cents for his wheat, a difference of five cents a bushel between these two states without any tariff wall at all. The Washington farmer received 78 cents a bushel for his wheat, or two cents a bushel less than we in Manitoba received for ours. The difference between the price that the Washington farmer received, 78 cents, and that which the Minnesota farmer received, 94 cents, is 16 cents a bushel. There is a far greater difference between these two states in the union than there is in the price that the Manitoba farmer receives and the price that the Dakota farmer receives.
We have had several speeches on this question. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) touched on the wheat question when he was speaking, and this is what he said in connection with it. You will find it in 'Hansard,' page 3730:
I do say this, however, that so far as I have been able to examine the matter-and I have looked into it with some care-I cannot see any reason why we should expect any very great increase in the price of wheat for exportation to the United States. There may be a reason, and there may be an increased price, but I am not able exactly to find out how it will come about.
Neither am I. I would like to quote also my hon. friend from Provencher (Mr. Molloy). He represents the next constituency to mine, he knows the conditions in Manitoba just as well as we do, and he has gone on record in connection with this wheat question. What does he say? ' Hansard,' at page 4267, he uses these words:
I do not pretend that it will increase the price of wheat to the Canadian producer, but I say it will maintain the present prices.
That is as far as he would go. That_ is as far as any man can expect to go with reference to this arrangement, but I want to tell you, Mr, Chairman, that I am not satisfied with maintaining the price at the present figure. I want to see the Manitoba farmers and the farmers of western Canada get a better price, and the way to do that is by the government owning and operating the terminal elevators. It will mean

two or three cents a bushel on all the grain grown in western Canada. More than that I have no hesitation in saying that if the government will own and operate the Hudson Bay railway it will add from four to six cents to the value of every bushel of grain we grow in western Canada. These are the things that I have voted for in this house; these are the things that hon. gentlemen opposite have voted against on every opportunity. In 1905 the amount of wheat produced in the three western provinces was 84,000,000; oats, 78,000,000 bushels; and barley 16,000,000 bushels. In 1908 the production amounted to, wheat, 147,000,000 bushels; oats, 197,000,000 bushels and barley 31,000,000 bushels. The increase in these three years was, wheat, 63,000,000 bushels; oats, 119,000,000 bushels, and barley 14,500,000 bushels. Saying nothing about the amount that we exported in 1905, but taking the amount of the increase alone, put these surplus products on the markets of the United States, and I want to ask you Mr. Chairman, or any fair-minded man, where will the price go in the United States? It is bound to go down; there is no doubt in the world about that. Why are the farmers in North Dakota rising at every point to protest against this deal? It is because they know the moment this deal goes through the premium that they have been receiving in the past will be wiped out, and their price will he put upon an export basis. I say, Mr. Chairman, that the proper policy for the people of Canada is to leave reciprocity alone, remedy the troubles we have at the present time and build Canada up, work out our own salvation and let the people of the United States do the same. I wish to read further the following statement by the Hon. P. C. Knox, and I quote from 'Reciprocity with Canada,' page 6. He says:
In providing for free wheat we also take into account the facilities which the United States possesses for handling a part of the surplus Canadian crop and thus preventing the demoralization of prices which results through the dumping of-large quantities upon the European markets, where the world's price is fixed. The free admission of grain from Canada thus meets the present situation and provides against future contingencies when the Canadian surplus becomes greater by placing the control in the hands of our own grain growers. They have no cause to fear a demoralizing influx under the conditions which will result from the reciprocity agreement.
At page 44, of this book Mr. Wilson, Secretary of Agriculture of the United States savs:
The United States produces surplus wheat above domestic requirements. This surplus production is sold in foreign countries. The price of our exported surplus is governed by the world's requirements, being regulated by Mr. SHARPE (Lisgar).
the law of supply and demand, and the price of wheat in the United States while we are exporting, is governed by the price at which the surplus is sold, as a general proposition. Occasionally wheat corners may interfere with the law of supply and demand, and temporarily affect the price.
Distance from markets has much to do with the prices of grain. So this proposition is modified by proximity to markets and cost of transportation. While Canada is exporting wheat or other grains and the United States is also exporting wheat, there is no particular reason why Canadian wheat should come here, unless it be that a mixture of Canadian and American wheat may be desirable on the part of our milling exporters, and our millers may find it profitable to handle the Canadian surplus. But the price to the Canadian for this surplus wheat will be substantially the same whether sold in Europe or the United States. However, if the handling of Canadian wheat iby United States railroads, merchants and mills has a tendency to reduce the price it will be reduced to Canadians; and if it should reduce the price of bread to the American consumer, wise statesmanship may find it necessary to do that to avoid greater evils.
At page 46 he says:
We can handle the Canadian export grain crop with facility. If it is brought inside our borders and milled, as it would he, our dairy men could use with great profit the byproducts of the mills. This is the feature-bran and shorts-that makes dairy products and robs the soil. If we cannot increase our yield to meet the demands cf increasing population, free wheat from the nearest fields would be desirable. The influences at work are enabling the American acre to produce more, but it is a question whether this increase will meet the requirements of our rapidly growing population. Wheat growing for sale from the farm, as the pioneer practises it, can only be temporary. The land refuses to yield profitable crops >after a few years, when recuperative farming must be resorted to to build up the soil where the soil robber has reduced it by grain growing. This is the reason the older prairie states, turn to grass, corn and domestic animals as soon as they can bring about the change. The United States could with great profit and benefit to the land take all the grains Canada has to sell and devote its land to less exorbitant crops, as is evidenced by the older prairie state farmers who grow no grain to sell, buy their flour and thereby keep up the fertility of the soil. In the western states where the farmer has turned from grain raising for sale to the production of crops to be fed to domestic animals on the farm, the new departure has become so profitable that lands in those states have risen in value to $100 and $200 per acre, and rents from $4 to $6 per acre.
I want to say, Sir, that I have the honour to represent one of the oldest constituencies in the province of Manitoba, and that is mighty good advice to the farmers of my constituency. We have been growing wheat crop after wheat crop in southern Manitoba, and we have come to a

time now when we must change our methods, and, therefore, it is that I say that the advice given by Mr. Wilson to the farmers of the United States west is mighty good advice to the farmers of my own constituency. Mr. J. J. Hill has had a good deal to say on this wheat question, and no one has studied it more closely than he. Speaking at St. Paul, Mr. Hill said:
Now, then, what will the imperial federation plan mean to the United States and how will it affect the wheat farmer of the northwest, or of any other section of the country? In the first place, there is this established fact: The surplus of any given commodity fixes its price. It is our surplus wheat we export that fixes the price of our wheat, and that price is fixed in the Liverpool market. That is true of everything we export.
As a local illustration, the difference between the price of wheat at [Minneapolis and in Winnipeg is about 5 cents in favour of the northwest. So far well and good. Reciprocity would not materially raise or lower that difference.
Suppose, now, that Canada joins the imperial federation of English colonies, as is proposed. A reasonable differential that England might impose on our wheat would be 15 cents a bushel, and that would mean our wheat growers would find their whole product lowered that much per bushel in value. The average crop is 700,000,000 bushels. Figure it out for yourself. And right on top of that we would face also this proposition: Great Britain would take over practically all of the $200,000,000 in round numbers that Canada now pays us for manufactured articles we export across the border,. then add the six hundred and more millions we export to Great Britain, and we find that, if we fail to adopt the reciprocity agreement with Canada and drive it to an imperial federation, we are cheapening our (wheat crop annually, say, 15 cents per bushel, and at the same time we are losing $800,000,000 of export business to England and Canada. Can we afford to do this? I say, no, and I think every man who gives this matter the study of the situation due it, will agree with me.
He wants us to step into the reciprocity deal and put it through on this side of the line and say good-bye to the mother land entirely. For my part I am not prepared to do it.
President Taft also made a speech at New York on April 27. He said:

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.

speechtext:
' I have said that this was a critical time in the solution of the question of reciprocity,' concluded the president. ' It is critical because unless it is now decided favourably to reciprocity it is exceedingly probable that no such opportunity will ever again come to the United States. The forces which are at work in England and in Canada will derive an impetus from the rejection of this treaty and if we would have reciprocity with all the advantages that I have described and that I earnestly and sincerely believe will follow its adoption, we must take it now or give it up for ever.'
That is the idea of President Taft. Representative George W. Prince, of Illinois, gave his version of this proposal, and I wish to read a few words from his speech:
I say to our neighbours on the north, be not deceived. When we go into a country and get control of it, we take it. It is our history, and it is right that we should take it if we want it, and you might as well understand it. The Speaker has so said; the party back of him has so said, and it does not deny that that is its desire. Now let us see if the people of Canada believe in reciprocity and annexation.
For my part I am not in favour of that kind of thing; I do not think it is the proper policy for us in this country. I say that we should keep on in the channels in which we have been working during the past 42 years, and build up this country in connection with the British Empire. They talk about opening the market of
90.000.	000, who are growing and exporting the same goods that we produce, only in larger quantities. If the government wanted to do anything for our farmers and open up new markets for the people of Canada, why did they not go to some importing countries that would have been of value to us? For instance Switzerland imported in 1908
12.000.	000 bushels of wheat, Japan 7,000,000 bushels, Italy 50,000,000 bushels, Germany
77.000.	000 bushels, Belgium 69,000,000 bushels, Sweden 7,600,000 bushels, France 13,000,000 bushels. These countries together imported 226,000,000 bushels of wheat in 1908. Here were markets that would have been some good to us, countries consuming just the goods that we have to export. But it is farthest from the minds of the government to open up a market that needs our goods, they want to open the markets of a fcountry that want to take our goods from us and make money in manufacturing them and re-exporting them
I say that, in my opinion, this is not in the best interests of the people of this country. I heard the Finance Minister say some time ago that this deal was made for the masses, and not for the classes, and I wondered at that time whether he remembered the masses when he was paying the classes $17,119,000 of the masses' money in bounties to the steel companies throughout this country. He forgot the masses when he was paying this $17,000,000 out, but now he turns the cry and says he is working for the masses. It is something new if he is.
In 1910, we produced in Canada farm crops amounting to $507,000,000, and dairy

products amounting to $98,000,000, a total of $605,000,000. We exported about $105,000,000 worth and we used at home about $500,000,000 worth of those products of the farm. I think that the home market is by long odds the most important market we have, because every bushel of grain that we consume at home takes that much from the markets of the world, and thereby just to that extent raises the world's price and every bushel that we export into the world's markets lowers'the price just that much. In 1910 we exported 52,000,000 worth of wheat. Of this $49,000,000 worth went to the British market and $3,000,000 went to other markets. In the same year we exported $1,107,000 worth of barley, of which $744,000 went to the British market and $363,000 went to other markets. In the same year we exported $21,607,000 worth of cheese. We sent to the British market $21,481,000 worth, and $126,000 worth went to other markets. It looks to me as though we had established markets now, and I think that we should remedy any troubles that we may now have, and keep on in the road that we are travelling. Who will benefit by this Bill if it does go through? I say that it will be the American paper trust, the Chicago beef trust, the United States steel company, the Minneapolis milling trusts and James J. Hill's railways. These are the companies and the trusts that will benefit by this Bill if we allow it to go through, not the grain growers of western Canada. When the grain growers were here on December 16 last, they asked for government ownership and operation of the terminal elevators, government ownership and operation of the Hudson Bay railroad, the establishment of a chilled meat trade, the extension of the British preference to 50 per cent, an amendment of the Banking Act and amendments of the Railway Act in connection with cattle guards, and live stock on railways and in relation to freight rates. They also asked for a Bill for the establishment of co-operative societies, and presented their resolution in connection with the tariff. I have worked for and voted for most of these things that they have asked for-in fact, all of them, except the tariff resolution.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: What does my hon. friend think should be done about the tariff?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I think there should be a permanent tariff commission appointed which would have absolute control of the tariff of this country. Look at the tariff question in western Canada. A few years ago we had a duty of 35 per cent on agricultural implements coming into that country. It is lowered to-day to 17} Mr. SHARPE (Lisgar).
per cent, but we are paying as much for our implements as we did when the duty was 35 per cent. I say there should be a permanent tariff commission appointed to have absolute control over the tariff of this country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Subject to parliament.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS - RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Of course, always subject to parliament. I wish to say that in my meetings in western Canada I have said that I am not a free trader. No man who has voted for me in either of the elections that I have run has ever heard me say anything in regard to free trade with the United States, because I want to say distinctly now that I do not think free trade is the proper policy for Canada at the present time. Take the history of all the great countries of the world to-day. Take England herself, take Germany, take France, take even the United States, what has built these countries up to what they are at the present time? Protection; there is no doubt about it. After they have had years of protection and have grown to what they are at the present time, ready to face the world, they are willing to have free trade with Canada, because they want to get ' control of ' the natural resources of this country. I say the policy of this country is protection-as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has said, adequate protection-all the way through. But we should have some arrangement whereby we can control the manufacturers of this country, and make them sell at a reasonable price to our people. This deal would allow us- I am speaking of my constituency-to benefit perhaps a little on cattle and barley; but we would lose on butter, eggs, cheese, pork of all kinds, mutton, horses, oats, vegetables, swine and sheep. Just take the egg question for a moment. When I was home, my partner, who is running our store, told me that on the 10th of March he went into the city of Winnipeg and offered some eggs he had for sale; and he found a man in Mr. Codville's wholesale house from the United States who offered to lay down eggs in Winnipeg for 21 cents a dozen. We paid 25 cents and were paying that to the farmers throughout my part of the country at that time; and this American offered to deliver absolutely fresh-laid eggs delivered in Winnipeg at 21 cents a dozen, after paying a duty of three cents a dozen and the freight. It meant that we would lose five cents a dozen on every dozen of eggs; and what happened? We had to sell eggs at 20 cents a dozen in our own town. The moment my partner went back to the town of Manitou, he had to put the price of eggs down to 20 cents, and the farmer was the loser. If the duty had been off eggs,

they would have been selling them at 17 cents instead of 20.
Now, to sum up. The right hon. the First Minister offers us reciprocity with the United States. He will open the markets of 90,000,000 people who do not want our goods at all, who are growing and exporting the very same goods that we are, and they will only export our goods if we send them over there. Why can't we do it ourselves? I say the policy of Canada is to manufacture these and export them ourselves. Now, what does the Conservative party offer in opposition to that? What have I said, in my feeble way, ever since I have been in this House, and what principle does the Conservative party stand for to-day in opposition to this infernal pact called reciprocity? We as a party stand for government ownership and operation of terminal elevators; government ownership and operation of the Hudson Bay railway; the establishment of a chilled meat trade throughout western Canada; a permanent tariff commission; putting Manitoba on an equal footing with the other provinces of the Dominion. We also will work for and stand for preferential trade within the empire. We will hold Canada for the Canadians. We will welcome all who will come to Canada; but we absolutely refuse to send the prosperity of this country out to others. If they want to enjoy the prosperity of this country, they must come to Canada. Why, Mr. Chairman, the government went into this deal without knowing anything about what they were doing. They had no prices of wheat, horses, cattle or anything along these lines in the different provinces of the Dominion or in the different states of the union. That is proven quite conclusively by the returns brought down some time ago. My brother, the member for North Ontario, asked for a statement showing the average prices of butter and eggs in London, England, for the past five years, in comparison with the prices respectively in the eastern provinces, in Montreal, in Toronto, in Minneapolis, in Chicago, in Detroit, in Buffalo, in Boston and in New York. And this is the answer he received:

This proves conclusively that they knew nothing about prices, and in every case where we have put them into a corner it has been shown that they knew absolutely nothing of the facts relating to these matters. The Postmaster General (Mr. Le-mieux) proved that conclusively some time ago when he was talking about the lobster question. He told the House what a great thing free lobsters would be for the people engaged in that industry in the maritime provinces until I understand the hon. member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) informed the hon. gentleman that lobsters had been on the free list in the United States for a good many years.
I have tried in my feeble way to show to you, Mr. Chairman, and to this House, my ideas of this deal, and the reasons why I cannot see my way clear to support it. And I believe that the people of my constituency will back me up and give me a better majority than before. For the reasons I have given I cannot see my way clear to support this proposition.
Mr. TAYLOR (Leeds) moved that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

Motion agreed to, and progress reported.
Mr. FISHER moved the adjournment of the House.

I wish to give notice that, when the House is next moved into Committee of Ways and Means or Committee of Supply, to-morrow, I will move an amendment:
That all the words after the word ' that ' in the proposed motion be omitted and tho following substituted therefor:-
This House regrets that in permitting the Farmers' Bank of Canada to commence and to continue business, the Minister of Finance and the Treasury Board failed to exercise such proper care and to take such reasonable precautions as were necessary to prevent evasion of the law and to protect the public interest.
